Το έκανε αυτό για έξι χρόνια, από τότε που η οικογένειά του διέφυγε από την καταστολή των Ροχίνγκια από τον στρατό της Μιανμάρ το 2017. «Μπορούμε τώρα να χρεώσουμε…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Every morning in the camp at Teknaf, Bangladesh, Mohammed Saber climbs to the roof of his family’s bamboo-and-tarpaulin home and sets out a single rectangular solar panel. He has done this for six years, since his family fled the Myanmar military’s crackdown on the Rohingya people in 2017. “We can now charge our phones, cook with light, children can study at night and use fans during the hot season,” says Saber, 35. A small panel on a makeshift roof, and an entire household runs on it. The same thing is happening in camps and disaster zones around the world. Solar has been edging into humanitarian response for years; what’s shifted is how seriously organizations are taking it, less as an experiment and more as something people actually need. From lanterns to cook stoves The range of what “solar kit” means is wider than it might sound. Sarah Rosenberg-Jansen , a research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute , describes the category as spanning solar lanterns, torches, and heating pads to full solar home systems and electric cook stoves . The common thread is portability and independence from the grid, which matters most when infrastructure is gone and things are moving fast. “In emergency situations , solar kits can be deployed immediately,” she says. That’s playing out across multiple places at once. In Karachi, Doctors Without Borders runs a tuberculosis clinic on solar power. In South Sudan’s Renk County , the UN migration agency installed solar-powered water filtration for families displaced by the war in neighboring Sudan. When Nepal’s floods killed 1,455 people and left 5,285 missing in August, local and international organizations distributed solar kits to survivors cut off from the grid. In Ukraine, a nonprofit called Hope For Ukraine has provided kits to thousands of families living through a war, including older residents who adapted without trouble. “We have grandmas and grandpas who are around 75 to 80 years old receiving kits,” says CEO Yuriy Boyechko. “It’s just a matter of plug and play.” Why costs finally shifted Solar panels don’t carry the same price volatility as fossil fuels, which are expensive and difficult to transport into disaster zones under ordinary circumstances and near-impossible when infrastructure has been destroyed. Only a few decades ago, solar was a luxury technology. Mass manufacturing and steady advances in efficiency changed that, and the price drop put solar kits within reach of humanitarian budgets in ways they weren’t before. Funding cuts and the waiting list What’s slowing things down now isn’t the technology. Aid organizations have long-running contracts built around diesel generators, and switching to solar means trusting new equipment, building new distribution chains, and sometimes doing that in genuinely hazardous conditions. Mark Gibson of the Global Platform for Action , a group promoting clean energy access, notes that the transition has been complicated for organizations with established logistics in place. Cuts to international donor funding have made it harder. Aimee Jenks, a program leader at GPA, was direct: “Much of the technical expertise in the humanitarian sector on energy has been cut. That’s now retracting a lot of progress.” Hope For Ukraine’s own numbers show how stretched the system is. By the end of 2026, the organization expects to have distributed more than 3,200 solar kits, a number that took two years to reach because of funding. “We have a waiting list of about 20,000 families,” Boyechko says. “We just cannot keep up with demand.” For Saber, the gap between what’s available and what people have isn’t an abstraction. His family has had their panel for six years, long enough to know exactly what changed. “It’s improved my family’s life,” he says. Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: The U.K.’s first “Flower Pharmacy” opened its doors last month — prescribing bouquets instead of medicine to those in need of a mood boost. The one-off experience in London was designed to encourage people to think differently about flowers, showing how they can play a role in everyday well-being rather than just being reserved for birthdays, anniversaries, and other special occasions. It was created in partnership with Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland and chartered horticulturist, TV gardener, and author David Domoney. Guests were matched with blooms tailored to their mood before leaving with a bouquet recommended to lift, calm, or energize them. For example, yellow flowers, including sunflowers, roses, freesias, and snapdragons, were prescribed to boost happiness, while calming bouquets featured blue and green blooms like hydrangeas, delphiniums, and chrysanthemums. For those who needed a dose of energy, there were also vibrant orange, red, and pink flowers. Courtesy of SWNS The event came as a poll of 2,000 British adults found 37% struggle when daylight saving time ends, with 29% admitting the time change leaves them feeling glum. Discussing the partnership with Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland, which commissioned the research and the pop-up, Domoney said: “There’s something incredibly uplifting about flowers, and research has shown that they can have a positive effect on our mood and emotional well-being. From the cheerful yellows of sunflowers and freesias to the calming tones of blues and greens, color can influence how we experience the spaces around us.” “We often associate flowers with special occasions, but there’s no reason we shouldn’t enjoy their beauty and the benefits of having them around us in everyday life,” he continued. “Sometimes, it’s the simplest connections with nature that can make a real difference to how we feel.” Courtesy of SWNS The survey also found that around a third of respondents spend more time indoors following the clock change, while 28% find the darker evenings difficult and 22% experience lower energy levels. The good news? There are plenty of ways to lift that low mood, like listening to music, reading a book, exercising, spending time in nature and, yes, buying flowers. While just 9% of people said they regularly treat themselves to blooms, the emotional response to receiving them is clear — half said they feel happy after being presented with a bouquet, 45% grateful, 34% joyful, and 24% comforted. Courtesy of SWNS Monique Kemperman, horticulture expert for Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland, said: “As the days become shorter and darker, small acts of self-care can make a real difference, and flowers are a simple way to bring color, joy, and positivity into everyday life.” “Our research shows just how much of an emotional impact they can have, yet many people still reserve them for somebody else or a special occasion,” she added. “The Flower Pharmacy is about encouraging people to see flowers as an everyday well-being boost rather than a treat.” This article was originally written by Jasmine Lenthall for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s a particular kind of motivation that kicks in around the holidays. You think: this year, I’m going to do something. You picture yourself in an apron at a soup kitchen, and it feels good. The problem is that a lot of other people are picturing the same thing at the same time. Most food banks and soup kitchens see volunteer demand spike around Thanksgiving , sometimes to the point where they have more help than they can use on that one day. If you want your time to count, a little strategy goes a long way. The good news: there are 17 solid options below, and several of them work whether you have four hours, four minutes, or no desire to leave your couch. National organizations with locations near you These programs operate across all 50 states, so wherever you are, there’s likely a chapter close enough to walk in. Feeding America Feeding America runs the largest hunger-relief network in the country. If you want to volunteer at a food bank on Thanksgiving, call ahead first. Holiday demand often fills slots fast, and some locations redirect walk-ins toward future dates when the need is more consistent. Meals on Wheels Meals on Wheels delivers hot meals to seniors who can’t get out on their own. The flexibility here is part of the appeal: you can sign up for a single delivery route or build it into a regular habit. The Salvation Army The Salvation Army works across a wide range of needs, from veterans to abuse survivors to people experiencing homelessness. There’s almost always something useful you can do, even on short notice. Operation Turkey Operation Turkey runs a tightly organized four-hour shift from 8 a.m. to noon, packing meals for homeless individuals. If you want a defined commitment with a clear end time, this is a good fit. Feed My Starving Children Feed My Starving Children packs meals at permanent sites in Arizona, Illinois, Minnesota, and Texas. It runs on a reservation system, so sign up before the week of. Toys for Tots Toys for Tots runs its drives through December, so Thanksgiving week is peak season. Volunteer slots exist for collection drives, not just drop-offs. Goodwill Goodwill often looks for people who can share a professional skill, not just sort donations. If you have a background in workforce development, finance, or career coaching, that’s where you’d fit in. United Way United Way sponsors a range of community initiatives, including garden planting, literacy programs, and neighborhood projects. What’s available depends on your city, so look up your local chapter. Local options that don’t require a national signup Soup kitchens and community meal programs often run on the same skeleton crew year after year. A call a week ahead is usually all it takes. Animal shelters are another option, especially if you’re better with dogs than crowds. Staff still work on Thanksgiving, and extra hands for walks or socialization are usually welcome. If you’re up for something more active, turkey trots are 5K races held in communities across the country on Thanksgiving morning, with proceeds going to local charities. You walk or run, and the entry fee does the work. The National Park Service also coordinates trail maintenance and cleanup projects throughout the fall. Check the volunteer page for your nearest park. If you can’t leave the house Gift-a-Family Gift-a-Family lets you sponsor a family through their holiday wishlist. The sign-up deadline is November 30, so there’s still time. Homefront America Homefront America directs donations toward grocery and turkey vouchers for military families. Support Our Troops Support Our Troops coordinates handwritten letters to deployed service members. It takes about ten minutes and goes a long way. One thing to know before you go Holiday volunteering is genuinely good, but the reality is that organizations often need year-round help. Of course, showing up once during the holidays could be the gateway to showing up regularly. If you get redirected on Thanksgiving Day because a food bank is at capacity, ask when they need people most. Often the answer is right after the holiday rush! Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: Most of us have a pretty good sense of who we think Gen Xers are and how they were raised: the latchkey kids who raised themselves, drank from the hose, and came in for dinner when the streetlights came on because their Boomer parents were either stuck at work or totally hands-off. But not all Gen Xers were raised by Baby Boomer parents . A sizable chunk, and even some older Millennials, had parents who were born a little bit earlier. This generation of parents, the Silent Generation , had a noticeably different approach. Some Gen Xers were raised by Silent Generation parents Your typical member of Generation X was born in the mid to late ’60s through around 1980, making most of them around 46-61 years old today. Typically, we think of Gen Xers as being raised by the Baby Boomers, who were in their 20s and 30s for most of that time period. But there’s a small slice of time, a few years in the mid-1960s, when it was actually a different generation having most of the kids: The Silent Generation. The Silent Generation refers to people born right smack in the middle of the Great Depression or near the beginning of World War II. It’s a generation that gets far less discussion than others, partly because it’s small, comprising only around 50 million people in the United States. The depression and the war caused birth rates to plummet, which, of course, set the stage for the “boom” of the Baby Boomers after WWII ended. But the Silent Generation grew up in notoriously harsh times, which strongly shaped how a handful of older Gen Xers were raised. Hallmarks of Silent Generation parents How was growing up with Silent Generation parents different than being raised by Boomers? Extreme thriftiness The Silent Generation was born and came of age in some of the leanest times our country has ever seen. Whether it was the Great Depression or wartime rationing, they had to make the absolute most of what they had. Those penny-pinching habits followed them well into their life as parents raising a family. “We weren’t allowed to take a shower, because my dad thought it would raise the water bill. So my sister and I had to take baths, and we had to share bath water,” TheOver50Woman shares about her parents on TikTok. “That’s probably the reason I’m a raging, raging germaphobe.” Gen Xers also add that the Silent Generation was the ultimate “finish everything on your plate” generation. GenXJono on YouTube quipped, imitating his own parents, “ You no like your food? I didn’t have food! Or a mother to make it for me!” Gen Xers raised by Silent Generation parents report getting very little in the way of toys or clothes that weren’t hand-me-downs, and that snacking between meals was usually forbidden and seen as wasteful. Heads down While Boomers came of age in the 1960s, a time of social rebellion, the Silent Generation grew up in far more conservative times. The ’50s were all about conformity, traditional gender roles, and a return to normalcy after the war. The Silent Generation was raised to work hard, keep their head down, and toe the company line. It follows, then, that they often had little tolerance for children’s whining, crying, or squabbles. This is the generation that coined the terms “Children should be seen, not heard” and “I’ll give you something to cry about.” A commenter on TheOver50Woman’s video writes, “Opinions against the grain were seen as silly and attention seeking. Crying? My parents used to sing ‘crybaby Becky, crybaby Becky’ and get other children to do the same.” They also tended to show affection by providing food and shelter rather than with words or physical touch. Another commenter added, “In college, I stayed a weekend at a friend’s house with his parents. It was a revelation: I didn’t realize that other mothers hugged their children.” If Boomers were about climbing the ladder and reaching new heights of achievement, the Silent Generation was the lunch-pail type—show up, work hard, and don’t complain until it’s time to retire. Those values showed up in how they raised their kids. No time for leisure Growing up during the Great Depression or World War II, the Silent Generation didn’t have much time for leisure. If they weren’t working, scavenging, or helping around the house, their very survival was at stake. It’s another habit they carried into adulthood. TheOver50Woman shares, “We were not allowed to sit during the day. This was not up for debate, you always had to be doing something. Chores were not an option and we certainly didn’t get paid to do them.” It’s a strong contrast to the stereotypical Gen X upbringing, where a single parent or both parents were out of the house working, leaving the kid to roam the neighborhood, play Nintendo, or practice with their rock band all day. Many Gen Xers raised by the Silent Generation had to get jobs as soon as they could and use that money to contribute to the household. Resilience & family-first Some Gen Xers report that their Silent Generation parents were often emotionally distant and demanding, but this generation had many admirable qualities as well. For example, many survived extremely harsh childhoods and passed that resilience on to their children. They passed down frugal Great Depression recipes; kids learned practical skills like gardening and home repair, and they had little to no sense of “keeping up with the Joneses.” Maureen Hennessy on TikTok says, “Our vacations were visiting family… We didn’t stop for food, we didn’t get a hotel. And I really wouldn’t have it any other way because … they were smart to make sure that they used their resources and didn’t set us up for failure. My Gen Z kids have grown up with stuff , we could fill landfills. If I could go back and do it over again, I’d raise them the way I was raised.” The Silent Generation is also known for being selfless and willing to sacrifice for the good of the family. Many Gen Xers raised by these parents have eventually come to appreciate how hard they worked. Gen X is known as the latchkey kids, the laissez-faire slackers, the MTV generation. But that reputation doesn’t paint a full picture, and it certainly doesn’t describe all Gen Xers, especially not the older ones raised by Silent Generation parents. If Boomer parents were hands-off and lenient, the Silent Generation was far stricter and more demanding overall. Whatever they lacked in emotional openness and warmth, they made up for it—at least in part—with a self-sacrificing work ethic that ensured their kids could survive anything, just like they did. The post Gen Xers share what it was like being raised by Silent Generation parents instead of Boomers appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Οι Elder Millennials δεν είχαν το Διαδίκτυο μέχρι τα «χρόνια διαμόρφωσης» τους. Τους έδωσε ένα τεράστιο πλεονέκτημα.
items.titleOriginal: Elder Millennials didn’t have the Internet till their ‘formative years.’ It gave them a huge advantage.
items.description: Οι Millennials που γεννήθηκαν στις αρχές της δεκαετίας του '80 μπορεί να έχουν φτάσει στο γλυκό σημείο μεταξύ της σύγχρονης τεχνολογίας και της καθημερινής ζωής. Το κλειδί; Ήταν να μάθουν να προσαρμόζονται καθώς μεγάλωναν στην ενηλικίωση. Ονομάζονται elder Millennials, κάτι που είναι ένα σημείο κόλλημα για ορισμένους. Στην πραγματικότητα, η Erica Dhawan, μια εμπειρογνώμονας ηγεσίας, ονόμασε για πρώτη φορά αυτή τη μικρογενιά «γηριατρική» Millenni…
items.descriptionOriginal: Millennials born in the early ’80s may have hit the sweet spot between modern technology and everyday life. The key? It was all about learning to adapt as they grew into adulthood. They’re called elder Millennials, which is a sticking point for some. Actually, Erica Dhawan, a leadership expert, first called this microgeneration “geriatric” Millennials, which some found even more egregious. But labels aside, this group fell between the quieter world of Boomers and Gen Xers and the noisier dial-up sounds of the ’90s. This often gave elder Millennials a clear advantage in getting the best of both worlds. Childhood without the internet Like their Gen X cousins, elder Millennials grew up without the internet or cell phones. This lack of constant scrolling and/or being reachable at all times rooted them in some ways, like encouraging more playtime outside. But unlike Gen X, many of whom didn’t get online until they were already young adults, elder Millennials could learn new tech as it grew and evolved. In a piece for Fortune , Success Editor Hillary Hoffower explains the “four types of Millennials.” She mentions Dhawan and explains that, from a workplace standpoint, they have it all. “This early ’80s cohort, on the cusp of Gen X, was the first to grow up with PCs in their homes but also feels comfortable with TikTok,” she (Dhawan) wrote. “Because they straddle the line between digital native and digital adapter, she believes they can bridge the divide between older and younger workers in the workplace, teaching both traditional body language and digital skills.” Tale of two cities Hoffower then quotes Jason Dorsey, president of the Center for Generational Kinetics : “In this way, the ‘geriatric Millennial’ microgeneration is a bit more like Gen X ‘because they sort of have the wind at their back and had more of a foothold than the segment of Millennials right after them,’ Dorsey says. While they still struggled with high student debt, this stronger footing put them in a better financial position to pay their loans. This is where he says the ‘tale of two cities’ of Millennials emerges.” In a post on X, user @HardPass4 sums up exactly why elder Millennials so often thrive: “An elder Millennial is one who grew up without the internet or cell phones, it all arrived in our formative years, which allowed us to retain the necessary social skills to learn the technology without it becoming a crutch, therefore making us into productive members of society.” ‘Hella adaptable’ The post’s comments lit up like a fire. One explains, “Basically we’re Gen X that learned technology.” Another points out the adaptability aspect: “It also made most of us hella adaptable because no standard stayed around for long.” Another X user completely agrees and compares it to younger Gen Xers. “100%. It’s also why younger/mid Gen X can sit down with various machine learning tools and get crazy output and then be able to communicate and put the knowledge to work with other people. Working at Arby’s gave more real skills than coding camp.” Feeling their feelings For the record, some Millennials have come up with what they feel are better terms than “geriatric” or “elder” Millennials. Reporter Lizzy Acker shares in The Oregonian that it has always rubbed her the wrong way. “As a person born in 1982, I would like to object to this classification, mainly because I am not old and am still annoyed about my ‘geriatric’ pregnancy a year and a half ago, but also because I don’t like the way it makes me feel and isn’t that, feeling your feelings, a lot of what being a Millennial is all about?” Her suggestions include the Oregon Trail Generation, the Home Alone Generation, the Book It Generation, and yep…just plain Millennial. The post Elder Millennials didn’t have the Internet till their ‘formative years.’ It gave them a huge advantage. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Passengers had to restrain their own pilot mid-flight. The co-pilot was left to land the plane alone.
items.description: Ο Rodney McDonald πετούσε με τη σύζυγό του και τους δύο γιους του όταν το αεροπλάνο τράνταξε δυνατά στη μία πλευρά. Μετά το έκανε ξανά. «Τη στιγμή που το αεροπλάνο παρέσυρε, ήξερα ότι κάτι δεν πήγαινε καλά γιατί δεν ήταν αναταράξεις», είπε ο McDonald στο ABC News. «Πραγματικά ένιωθα ότι κάποιος είχε τραντάξει τα χειριστήρια και μετά συνέβη ξανά και ξανά». Τα αγόρια του άρχισαν να προσεύχονται…
items.descriptionOriginal: Rodney McDonald was flying with his wife and two sons when the plane jerked hard to one side. Then it did it again. “The moment the plane swerved, I knew something was wrong because it was not turbulence,” McDonald told ABC News . “It really felt like someone had jerked the controls, and then it happened over and over again.” His boys started praying . Air Canada flight AC7664 on June 24 was a regional run from Newark, New Jersey, to Halifax, Nova Scotia, operated by PAL Airlines on a De Havilland Q400 turboprop with 61 passengers aboard. Something had gone wrong in the cockpit. “One of the flight attendants entered the cockpit frantically, and a few moments later, he was dragging one of the pilots out of the cockpit onto the aisleway of the airplane,” McDonald said. The captain appeared to be having a seizure. He wasn’t violent, McDonald said, but he clearly had no control over his body, and in a narrow aisle on a moving plane, that was its own danger. McDonald and about four other passengers moved in, with a registered nurse on board directing them. “It was a fairly strenuous 40 minutes of keeping him down and using as many seatbelts as we could to restrain his legs, arms, and chest,” McDonald said. Medical guidance usually runs the other way. The CDC advises against holding down someone having a seizure, recommending instead that they be turned onto their side with the area cleared and their airway kept open. The passengers were working under a nurse’s direction, with little room and nowhere to go. Up front, the first officer was alone on the plane. He diverted to Boston Logan, where Massachusetts State Police said the plane landed around 1:40 p.m. after a crew member reported the medical emergency. Emergency responders met the aircraft, and the captain was taken to a hospital. Passengers told WABC that he seemed to come back to himself around the time they touched down. Air Canada said the captain was removed from the flight deck under safety protocols and noted that its pilots are trained to fly and land without a second pilot. The airline hasn’t said what caused the episode, and it hasn’t made any public update on the captain’s condition. The passengers did make it to Halifax. The flight left Boston that evening and landed safely, only about seven hours behind schedule. The post Passengers had to restrain their own pilot mid-flight. The co-pilot was left to land the plane alone. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Οι δημιουργοί του «Curious George» δραπέτευσαν από τους Ναζί κατά τη διάρκεια του Β' Παγκοσμίου Πολέμου με ποδήλατα, κουβαλώντας πρωτότυπα χειρόγραφα
items.titleOriginal: ‘Curious George’ creators escaped Nazis during WWII on bicycles, carrying original manuscripts
items.description: Το Curious George είναι μια από τις πιο αγαπημένες σειρές παιδικών βιβλίων του 20ου αιώνα. Δημιουργήθηκε από κοινού από την ομάδα συζύγων H. A. και Margret Rey. Σύμφωνα με τη βιογραφία τους, ο H. A. ήταν κυρίως υπεύθυνος για τις ιδέες και τις εικονογραφήσεις, ενώ η Margret δημιούργησε τις πλοκές της ιστορίας και έκανε περισσότερο τη συγγραφή. Αλλά ο περίεργος Τζορτζ δεν θα έφευγε…
items.descriptionOriginal: Curious George is one of the most beloved children’s book series from the 20th Century. It was co-created by the husband-and-wife team H. A. and Margret Rey. According to their biography , H. A. was mostly responsible for the ideas and illustrations, while Margret created the story plots and did more of the writing. But Curious George would not exist today if the couple had not escaped the Nazis during World War II. The Reys were both German Jews and had been living in Paris, France, at the start of the war. When the Nazis invaded Paris, they made a daring and courageous escape on bicycles with their creative works in hand. H. A. and Margret Rey’s story H. A. (Hans Augusto Rey) and Margret (born Margarete Elisabeth Waldstein) were both born in Hamburg, Germany. They met in childhood but didn’t begin a relationship until they were both living and working in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in 1935. H. A. worked for his family’s bathtub business, and Margret moved there to escape Germany’s political climate and Hitler’s rise to power . Both were artists. Margret studied art at the Bauhaus, and Hans grew up drawing. In Rio de Janeiro, they started the city’s first advertising agency. They married on August 16, 1935. After spending time in Paris during their honeymoon in 1936, the couple decided to move there. Escaping the Nazis While living in Paris, H. A. illustrated and published many children’s books in England and France that featured his illustrations. He earned a French patent for his books that featured cut-out-and-fold animals. In 1939, the character of Curious George was born. Originally called Fifi, he appeared in the book titled Raffy and the 9 Monkeys . By the spring of 1940, however, it became clear that Hitler and the Nazis would invade Paris. The Reys escaped Paris on two bicycles that H. A. had pieced together using spare parts in the early morning hours of June 14, 1940. They carried only a few things—including five manuscripts, one of which would later become Curious George . After four days of biking, using updated Brazilian passports, they boarded a train in Orleans, France, to the French-Spanish border. From there, they traveled to Lisbon, Portugal, then back to Brazil. They moved to New York City in late 1940, where they started a new life publishing children’s books. Margret shared her first-hand account in an article titled, “ Times of Their Lives: Nine Authors and Illustrators Look Back on Significant Chapters from Their Illustrious Careers “: “In June 1940, on a rainy morning before dawn, a few hours before the Nazis, entered, we [Margret and her husband, H. A. Rey] left Paris on bicycles, with nothing but warm coats and our manuscripts–Curious George among them–tied to the baggage racks, and started pedaling south. We finally made it to Lisbon, by train, having sold our bicycles to customs officials at the French-Spanish border. After a brief interlude in Rio de Janeiro, our migrations came to an end one clear, crisp October morning in 1940, when we saw the Statue of Liberty rise above the harbor of New York, and we landed in the U.S.A. We took a small apartment in New York’s Greenwich Village, rolled up our sleeves, and were ready to start from scratch. We did not know a single publisher, but before the week was over we had found a home for Curious George at Houghton Mifflin. Among children, we seem to be known as the parents of Curious George. “I thought you were monkeys too,” said a little boy who had been eager to meet us, disappointment was written all over his face.” Publishing Curious George books The couple quickly settled in and secured a 4-book contract with publisher Houghton Mifflin in February 1941. The first Curious George book featuring the mischievous monkey was published later that year, and the couple went on to publish seven Curious George books together through 1966. Margret shared that the couple worked hard together. “We write and rewrite, we draw and redraw, we fight over the plot, the beginning, the ending, the illustrations—as a matter of fact, our work is nearly the only thing we do fight about,” she said . However, Margret’s name did not initially appear on the Curious George covers. She shared, “When we first came to America, our publisher suggested we use my husband’s name because the children’s book field was so dominated by women. They thought it would sell better. After a time, I thought, ‘Why the devil did I do that?’ so since then my name has appeared also.” (Both their names appeared in 1944 .) H. A. Rey died on August 26, 1977, just before Curious George ‘s biggest popularity boom, following a 1978 animation deal that brought Curious George to American TV and film. Margret died on December 21, 1996. Over 100 million copies of Curious George books have been sold worldwide today. The post ‘Curious George’ creators escaped Nazis during WWII on bicycles, carrying original manuscripts appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Οι θεραπευτές γάμου μοιράζονται τις 7 μεγαλύτερες κόκκινες σημαίες στις σχέσεις και πώς να τις αντιμετωπίσετε
items.titleOriginal: Marriage therapists share the 7 biggest red flags in relationships and how to deal with them
items.description: Οι άνθρωποι συχνά κατηγορούν την «έλλειψη επικοινωνίας» για συζυγικά προβλήματα, κάτι που είναι κατανοητό. Αφού έχουν την ίδια διαμάχη ξανά και ξανά, τα ζευγάρια μπορεί να υποθέσουν ότι δεν έχουν καταφέρει να ακούν ή να μοιράζονται αποτελεσματικά τα συναισθήματά τους. Αλλά μερικές φορές, η επικοινωνία δεν είναι το πρόβλημα. Σε ένα viral νήμα του Reddit, ζητήθηκε από τους θεραπευτές να σ…
items.descriptionOriginal: People often blame a “lack of communication ” for marital problems , which is understandable. After having what feels like the same argument over and over, couples might assume they haven’t mastered listening or sharing their feelings effectively. But sometimes, communication isn’t the problem. In a viral Reddit thread , therapists were asked to share the biggest relationship red flags they have seen in practice. Their responses indicated that an underlying dynamic often helps or hurts communication and, therefore, the marriage. While Reddit comments obviously aren’t a substitute for professional relationship advice, several of the therapists’ observations align with ideas in established couples therapy approaches and relationship research. Here are some of the relationship red flags that therapists say deserve a closer look. 1. Not working on self-regulation Man unable to regulate his emotions. Photo credit: Canva One couples therapist argued that, by and large, couples already know how to communicate effectively. What they don’t have a handle on is managing their own emotions. “I am a couples therapist. Every couple I work with comes in wanting to work on communication. I tell them that I can give them all of the fancy tools in the world, and I do have tools that I will give them to communicate well, but my guess is they know how to communicate. They very likely communicate well with many people in their lives. The work will be understanding what makes it so difficult to communicate well in this relationship now. The first thing I work on with every couple is actually self-regulation, which includes a willingness to regulate yourself. Consistent inability (ex: untreated mental health or hormonal issues) or unwillingness (ex: resentment, ego) to regulate yourself will ruin your marriage. If we can’t look at and address issues of self-regulation, nothing will change.” Research supports the broader idea that emotional regulation matters in relationships. A 2026 study of 174 couples in couples therapy found that emotional regulation difficulties were associated with relationship satisfaction for both individuals and their partners. That doesn’t mean couples need to suppress their emotions or never get angry. Self-regulation can be as simple as recognizing when you’re too overwhelmed to have a productive conversation and taking a break before saying something you’ll regret. 2. Waiting too long to go to therapy Anxious couple in therapy session. Photo credit: Canva Another therapist warned against waiting until a relationship is already in serious trouble before seeking professional help. “Therapist, though not a marriage therapist. There is a joke that if the wife is the one seeking therapy, there is a good chance the marriage will survive. If it’s the husband, then it’s already too late. The underlying understanding is that women will initiate counseling when there is a problem, but husbands often refuse. By the time they’re willing to go, it’s a last-ditch effort, but the wife is already out the door mentally. This is obviously a generalization, but if your partner mentions counseling, take that as a sign of a problem, rather than dismissing it as something you don’t need.” The gender generalization here needn’t be taken as a universal rule. Still, the larger point is worth considering: don’t assume couples therapy is only for couples on the verge of divorce. Research has found that couples with different levels of difficulties can benefit from couples therapy, meaning there isn’t one particular type of struggling couple who is “right” for treatment. 3. Letting romance die Bored couple on awkward date. Photo credit: Canva Relationships rarely collapse overnight from a single cataclysmic event. More often, partners gradually let their connection slip down the priority list. As one commenter put it: “They stop dating each other.” It’s short, but nevertheless true. There’s a reason that Drs. John and Julie Gottman emphasize that continuing to “date” your spouse (treating your partner with the same curiosity, intentionality, and romance you had at the beginning) is vital to keeping long-term relationships alive. “Dating” doesn’t have to mean making reservations at an expensive restaurant every Friday night. It can mean doing something fun together, asking what your partner cares about, or making time to be affectionate when there’s no household problem to solve. 4. Assuming negative intent Man lashing out at woman in anger. Photo credit: Canva One therapist argued that couples can get stuck when past hurts and resentment affect how they interpret each other’s behavior. “More than anything, it comes down to unregulated trauma and selfishness respectively hijacking the ability to regulate and use Positive Perspective. Positive Perspective means remembering who you married, why you chose them, that they’re a good person, and that unless they’re a legitimate abuser (rare), they aren’t trying to hurt you and would likely never want you to feel or tell yourself what you’re feeling/telling yourself about them or their love for you. I teach my couples intent and impact. In non-abusive relationships, assume positive (or at worst, neutral/unaware) intent when it comes to your partner’s actions or words, and be willing to accept and acknowledge/apologize for negative impact when it comes to your own. The more we can get a hold of defensiveness and regulate ourselves to be humble and view our lover’s feedback as a gift on both ends, the healthier our marriage will be. -LMFT trained in Gottman, EFT, Attachment etc ” Obviously, that doesn’t mean ignoring genuinely harmful behavior or assuming every action is well-intentioned. Rather, it simply means leaving room for the possibility that an irritating comment was careless at worst, rather than malicious. 5. Using “I feel like” statements instead of “I feel statements Couple trying to express their feelings. Photo credit” Canva This therapist actually did point to a specific communication tip: pay attention to what comes after the words “I feel.” “I’m an LMFT, trained in Gottman, and tell people that whatever follows “I feel like…” is a thought describing how you see the situation. “ I feel ____ emotion” is what describes the feeling that describes your internal experience. Once couples see it and can use it in good faith to communicate, it can help them pivot so many smaller disagreements about perspective into conversations about experience.” It’s a simple but important tweak that gives the other person something concrete to respond to, rather than asking them to defend themselves against a character judgment. 6. Putting the onus on everyone else to do the work A couple pointing the finger at each other. Photo credit: Canva Couples therapy can give people tools, but the therapist can’t do the work for them. One counselor who works with high-conflict couples described what happens when clients expect the therapist to fix their partner instead of looking at themselves. “Counselor here that works with high-conflict couples, specializing in BPD. The thing that I’ve had to realize as the therapist in the room is, if they don’t want to change, they’re not going to. I can walk them to every precipice, I can hand them every tool, and if they don’t wanna do the work, they’re not going to. So much of the work takes place outside of the therapy room, and people seem to forget this. I’ve had husbands yell at me that they bring their wives to me so I can fix them, screaming this while refusing to work on their own borderline traits. I’ve had wives telling me that I need to hold their husbands accountable, as if it is solely my responsibility to ensure that this grown man understands what responsibility is. So much irony. I explained time and time again that I’m there to help with communication, to facilitate, to walk them through the difficult conversations and to interpret what’s being said so things don’t escalate. With some people, they’re not there to get better; they want to win at therapy and be told they’re right. Getting them to understand that that isn’t going to happen. It’s very difficult sometimes.” 7. Hoping to go back rather than move forward Couple hanging their marriage portrait on a wall. Photo credit: Canva Perhaps the most thought-provoking advice in the thread was about what couples should actually expect from therapy. “Going in [to therapy] expecting to ‘save’ a marriage is a sure-fire way to end in divorce. The marriage a couple comes in to save was already dead and was what ended you here. Marriage counseling is to decide if you want to leave or continue the relationship. And if you decide to continue the relationship, you need to figure out how to build a new marriage with the person sitting next to you, not the person you envisioned from X years ago. Because they are not that person and likely never were.” The fact that you can’t go back doesn’t have to be a bad thing. Research published by the American Psychological Association describes creating a “new relational experience” as an important part of therapy, giving couples an opportunity to explore patterns that have been getting in the way of their relationship and develop new ways of relating. Thinking of marriage as something finite to be saved or sacrificed, rather than built brick by brick, might not be the best approach. Bottom line: the work goes beyond learning to communicate Communication may be what couples notice first when a marriage starts to struggle, but it isn’t always what needs fixing first. Sometimes the harder work is understanding what is happening underneath the words and deciding what each person is willing to do differently. The post Marriage therapists share the 7 biggest red flags in relationships and how to deal with them appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Some people seem to get along with everybody. They make friends while sitting at the bar, have a nice conversation with the gas station attendant, and make a great first impression. What makes them so comfortable around other people? Is it natural charisma , good looks, or a warm smile? According to a study in the Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin , they all share the same trait: interpersonal warmth. Psychologists define interpersonal warmth as a combination of qualities, which include friendliness, trustworthiness, kindness, and a sense of positive intentions. The interesting thing about interpersonal warmth is that it’s paradoxical. If you express warmth when you meet someone new, they are more likely to like you. If you are reticent to express warmth, for fear of rejection, the other person is less likely to like you. The big takeaway is that in social actions, you get back what you put out there. More likable people consistently approach others as if they will be liked, and their assumption is often confirmed. People talking at a house party. Photo credit: Canva Warm personalities are more likable The researchers discovered how interpersonal warmth works by studying people introducing themselves on video and rating them for how warm, confident, and likable they appeared. They also studied men who approached an attractive woman after receiving a positive social cue. In both situations, the same pattern emerged: those who expected rejection were rated less likable, and those who expected acceptance came off as warmer and more likable. Woman laughing. Photo credit: Canva Unfortunately, this works against people who put up their guard because they fear rejection. When you meet people in a defensive posture, you’re more likely to be rejected, which becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. People have good reasons to protect themselves when meeting new people, whether it’s trauma or they’re socially uncomfortable; however, that approach perpetuates the problem. Likable people, like people The reciprocal nature of interpersonal warmth mirrors research by Albert “Van” Sloan, who studied 2,437 high school students to find the trait that makes certain kids popular in school. After asking students to list the people they liked, the researchers found that the most popular people also liked the most people. “Learn how to like,” communications expert Vanessa Van Edwards, who reviewed the study in her book, Captivate , shared on The Dan Buettner Podcast . “In fact, be free with your likes. The most popular kids were the ones who were first likers. In other words, they walked down the hallway, and they say, ‘Hey, Dan. Hey, Sarah. Hey, Joy.’ They’re the ones who walk into a class and be like, ‘Hey, you want to sit with me?’ They are inviters. They are likers. They are looking for good. And in that way, I think that we can train ourselves to be more likable by searching and hunting for likes.” Ultimately, it comes down to approaching people with warmth, kindness, open ears, and an open heart. That may not come naturally to everyone, but if you can muster the confidence to approach people like they’re already friends, chances are you’ve probably just made a new one. The post Why are some people universally liked? Researchers found they share the same personality trait. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: T he staff at Erik’s Ranch & Retreats has a saying: Sheets, towels and lives changed daily . Erik’s Ranch is a guest retreat where autistic people are concierges, guides, wranglers, cooks and more. Located on 230 acres of pristine pasture and wilderness near Livingston, Montana, the ranch is less than an hour from Yellowstone National Park. It offers horseback riding, fly fishing, nature hikes, history walks and experiences with ranch animals and wildlife — most led or assisted by paid neurodivergent “members,” most of whom also live on the property. The inspiration for Erik’s Ranch dates back to 2008, when founder Kathryn Nordberg was pondering how her son, Erik, whom she described as “a moderately functioning teenager with autism,” would live as an adult — and particularly what would happen when she was no longer around. Ranch manager Cameron Porter (in black hat) and member John Rekedal help a visitor from New Jersey mount her steed for a trail ride. Credit: Jodi Hausen “As someone challenged with expressive language, there weren’t very many opportunities for kids like him,” she said, sitting in the well-appointed kitchen of the ranch’s six-bedroom lodge. So she established a nonprofit with a boutique-style hotel in Edina, Minnesota, where, even after she’s gone, Erik and others like him can live, work and thrive. There, adults on the autism spectrum work and live independently and are guided by life coaches toward achieving personal goals like interviewing, equine or cooking skills; or setting up an Etsy page to sell their artwork. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Using a similar model, in 2014 Nordberg opened the Montana ranch, where not only employees on the spectrum benefit: She designed most of the cabins specifically for neurodivergent guests. Though anyone can appreciate the soothing atmosphere, it’s particularly accommodating for those on the spectrum, who sometimes experience sensory overload. The calmingly simple cabins provide awe-inspiring vistas of the surrounding mountains with little to no sign of human activity. Hardware was selected to close drawers, cabinets and doors with hardly a sound. Walls, furnishings and bedding are muted earth tones and lights have dimmers. Credit: Jodi Hausen Erik’s Ranch is run primarily by young autistic people, some of whom also live on the property. The ranch has unparalleled views of the Absaroka-Beartooth Mountains. Autistic and other neurodivergent people are often misunderstood and feel out-of-place, experiencing discrimination, social exclusion, bullying and other situations that can lead to low self-esteem. That — and an inexorable need to mask their differences — often results in depression and anxiety. Some studies indicate that people on the spectrum are four times more likely to experience major depression compared with the general population. “Depression, loneliness, lack of confidence, feeling isolated, rejected, and a lack of community and people who care is what Erik’s Ranch is working to minimize and eliminate,” Nordberg said. And it’s working. John Rekedal, 21, lives in Minnesota but just spent his first summer working at the Montana ranch. When he’s home, he works in a large production greenhouse. And though his coworkers there are understanding, he prefers the camaraderie of working with the ranch’s small staff amid the hush of the surrounding mountains. Jacob Thoresen fetches horses from a pasture in preparation for a trail ride. Thoresen has been working for Erik’s Ranch and Retreats for 10 years. Credit: Jodi Hausen “I’m a whole lot more inclined to work outside,” he said. “And I know everyone’s name. It’s more relaxed.” Cornell University autism researcher Leslie Shaw analyzed a national sample of autistic adults who could answer a survey unassisted and found that only about 53 percent were working in 2023. Furthermore, in 2024, people with cognitive disabilities (of which neurodivergence is a subset) were employed at less than half the rate of people without any disability, according to Cornell’s Northeast ADA Center . These low employment rates may be due to neurotypical employers’ lack of experience with and understanding of neurodivergent people leading to misaligned work assignments, confusion and a fraught or untenable work environment. On a recent late summer day in Montana, Jacob Thoresen, 33, was gearing up to lead a small group of guests on a trail ride. He has been working with the nonprofit for 10 years and splits his time between its two locations. In black cowboy hat and jeans, he walked back and forth across the dirt-floored indoor arena to a tack room, gathering saddles and bridles. He saddled horses while other members dutifully scooped and cleaned areas around the animals. Credit: Jodi Hausen Erik’s Ranch & Retreats is part of a growing trend of workplaces designed to integrate people with autism or other disabilities. Thoresen had other jobs before coming to Erik’s. He was a baggage handler at the Minneapolis-Saint Paul Airport and worked in retail and manufacturing. He even tried a desk job. “But,” he said with a smile, “that isn’t me.” Thoresen said he’s gained confidence working with Erik’s Ranch & Retreats. “If you would have met me 10 years ago, I would have been, like, I couldn’t be able to do anything independent and be trusted to actually get the work done,” he said. “This place is teaching me how to be independent. In this last year, I’ve grown more.” He still gets support, but staff, recognizing his achievements, have loosened the reins. “I’m having to rely more on myself to work on those independent skills,” he added. Hannah Jacobs (left) helps Zoe Markman put fresh linens on a bed in one of the guest cabins at Erik’s Ranch. Credit: Jodi Hausen When asked what he finds challenging about working at Erik’s Ranch, Thoresen said workdays can be inconsistent. At the Minnesota retreat, he completes the same tasks daily. On the ranch, daily schedules shift and sometimes he gets overwhelmed. “But I can move through it,” he said. “I attribute that to the staff that I work with and just practice. They do a good job of seeing [my overwhelm] and being like, okay. And that helps, you know. I’ve had too many employers in the past that have been like, ‘Oh, you’re not having a good day? Well, just go home.’” Over the years, Erik’s Ranch & Retreats has employed 27 autistic young adults — 19 in the last year. The goal, Nordberg said, is to serve 30 members regularly. The organization is part of a growing trend of workplaces designed to integrate people with autism or other disabilities. John Rekedal helps clean around the horses in the indoor arena before a trail ride. Credit: Jodi Hausen Not far from Erik’s Ranch, Special K Ranch in Columbus, Montana, provides living quarters and jobs in farming, ranching and gardening and contracts with area businesses to employ adults with developmental disabilities. Over in Jackson, Wyoming, Vertical Harvest integrates people with a wide array of disabilities into their operations growing lettuces, microgreens, tomatoes and basil. In a fully accessible greenhouse, Vertical Harvest operates on what’s known as the “Grow Well” model of employment : providing opportunities for workers to pursue passions by creating or placing them in positions that correspond to their strengths and aspirations, their likes and dislikes. In other words, adapting the workplace to the employee rather than the other way around. Although she hadn’t heard of Grow Well, Nordberg embraces its philosophy. It doesn’t always work out as planned, though. “Not everyone wants to learn hospitality,” she said. In fact, one autistic young man told her he wanted to be a “white hat hacker,” using his computer skills for good. But she didn’t have a role that fit his skills and aspirations. In other instances, however, a member’s passions can be integrated into ranch operations. Part-time member Zoe Markman shows off a colorful collection of eggs gathered from the hens in the coop behind her. Credit: Jodi Hausen Zoe Markman, a 21-year-old autistic woman from Bozeman, loves animals — particularly chickens. So when Markman started working part-time at the ranch, Nordberg built a chicken coop and populated it with more than a dozen hens whom Markman gave punny names: Chiquille O’Neal, Princess Layer and Hen Solo. On a recent workday, Markman gathered more than a dozen colorful eggs. Nordberg also helped Erik start a baking business making cookies, brownies, scones and banana bread. Erik is a visual learner and communicator, so Nordberg created a pictorial cookbook with step-by-step instructions. She marked bins of flour, sugar and other ingredients with pictures so Erik can do most of the work independently. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The ranch can currently house five members and has five cabins and the lodge for guests on its expansive property. So Nordberg has room to expand, and she’d like to. But finances and land-use regulations present barriers. It’s expensive running a guest ranch, though the costs are partly covered by guest fees and philanthropy. And area permitting will only allow for seven more cabins. “This will never be a huge operation,” Nordberg said. But she’s gratified knowing there are places for Erik and others like him to live, belong and find meaningful work. This story was supported in part by the Solutions Journalism Network’s HEAL Fellowship. items.descriptionOriginal: The GPS on your phone helps you find your way to a favourite restaurant, avoid traffic jams and take an unfamiliar road with confidence. It tells you where you are and helps you figure out where to go next . Now, imagine a similar guiding system inside an operating theatre, helping a surgeon navigate the delicate structures of the human brain or spine. That is the idea behind easyNav , an image-guided surgical navigation system developed by Bengaluru-based health-tech company HRS Navigation. Using medical images to map a patient's anatomy and track surgical instruments in real time, the technology helps surgeons understand where they are operating, particularly when working around sensitive nerves, blood vessels, and other critical structures. Founded in 2015 by Arpit Paliwal and Shweta Paliwal, HRS Navigation has developed an indigenous alternative to imported surgical navigation platforms. Its systems are now installed in more than 200 hospitals and have supported over 20,000 surgeries, according to the company. Using CT scans, easyNav creates a map of the patient's anatomy and tracks surgical instruments in real time. But the motivation behind the startup was not simply to build sophisticated medical technology. It was to address a question that Arpit encountered repeatedly: why should access to advanced surgical care depend so heavily on where a patient lives or how much they can afford? Why surgical precision needed to reach beyond metros An electronics engineer who also completed an executive programme at IIM Calcutta, Arpit spent around 11 years in an international role before deciding to build a medical technology company in India. His experience had given him an understanding of surgical navigation and the standards these systems needed to meet. It had also helped him recognise a gap in the market. Surgical navigation technology was already available internationally, but its adoption in India was constrained by more than the cost of purchasing a machine. Some imported systems required hospitals to buy recurring consumables for every procedure or upgrade their operating theatres to meet specific infrastructure requirements. For hospitals working with limited budgets, these expenses could make the technology difficult to sustain, particularly when treating patients who could not afford to pay much for surgery. Arpit recalls meeting families who were struggling to afford treatment. One interaction that stayed with him was that of a father who told him to proceed with his child's operation, saying he would sell his house to arrange the money. Surgical navigation helps doctors locate tumours and understand their proximity to critical nerves, blood vessels and other structures. "I have seen that kind of reality," he says, describing the experiences that motivated him to build something for India. For him, the problem was not a lack of medical expertise. It was that the tools available to support complex procedures were not always accessible to the hospitals and patients who needed them. Simply reducing the price of an imported system would not necessarily solve this problem . The technology also had to work within the realities of Indian hospitals. "You need to adapt your system to work with the requirements of Indian infrastructure," Arpit explains. That became a guiding principle for HRS Navigation. Starting with a small office and building its technology from the ground up, the founders set out to develop a system that could work with the equipment hospitals already had, without compromising on accuracy. It was a demanding undertaking in a field requiring extensive research, engineering, testing and regulatory compliance. Arpit says developing the technology from the prototype stage took years of work, including studying research papers and building the team's technical expertise at a time when many of today's AI tools were not available. The effort eventually led to easyNav , designed around two priorities: precision that meets demanding clinical requirements and adaptability that makes the system practical for Indian hospitals. How does a GPS for surgeons work? To understand the technology, consider what happens when someone drives through an unfamiliar city without navigation. They must rely on signboards, landmarks and their own judgement to decide which road to take. A GPS adds another layer of information, showing their position in relation to the route and helping them correct their direction as they move. Surgical navigation applies a comparable principle inside the operating theatre, using medical imaging rather than road maps. Before surgery, CT scans provide detailed images of the patient's anatomy. These images are used to create a reference for the procedure. During the operation, the navigation system tracks the position of surgical instruments and displays where they are in relation to that anatomy. HRS Navigation designed easyNav to work with existing operating theatre infrastructure, making adoption easier for hospitals. This gives the surgeon an additional way to check the instrument's position and trajectory, particularly when the target lies deep inside the body or close to structures that must be preserved. In brain surgery, for instance, the system can help a surgeon plan the route to a tumour and understand its relationship with important structures. In spine procedures, it can help determine the entry point and trajectory for placing screws. Dr Ranjit Deshmukh, consultant neurosurgeon at Sahyadri Hospital, Pune, explains that complex procedures have traditionally relied on anatomical landmarks, surgical experience and imaging during the operation to establish orientation. "Navigation provides an additional layer of anatomical guidance, helping the surgeon plan and execute these procedures with greater confidence ," he says. With easyNav , Dr Deshmukh says he can understand where his instruments are in relation to the patient's anatomy in real time. He particularly values this in complex brain surgeries involving deep-seated tumours, lesions near major blood vessels and procedures around the skull base. The technology can also support planning when a tumour lies close to functional areas of the brain. Information from techniques such as functional MRI and tractography can help surgeons understand these relationships and plan an approach that aims to remove as much of the tumour as safely possible while preserving critical functions. Importantly, navigation does not replace a surgeon's judgement or experience. Instead, it provides additional information to support decisions during critical stages of an operation. Dr Deshmukh says he has used international navigation platforms for around 15 years and finds easyNav comparable in ease of use and overall workflow. "Once a surgical team becomes familiar with the system, it integrates into the procedure without adding unnecessary complexity," he adds. easyNav uses CT scans to create a 3D map of a patient's anatomy and infrared cameras to track surgical instruments in real time. He has also noticed a reduction in uncertainty during many complex cases, although he cautions that complications and revision rates depend on several factors and cannot be attributed to a single technology. For Arpit, maintaining this precision while making the system affordable required extensive research into components, performance, and design. The team worked to meet international quality and regulatory parameters while developing a system suited to the infrastructure and needs of its intended users. From a small-town hospital to a mother's second chance The value of this approach becomes clearer when the technology reaches hospitals beyond major metropolitan centres. Arpit recalls a surgeon in a small town in Maharashtra who used the system to operate on a young child from a farming family. The family had limited financial resources, and the surgeon operated for around Rs 10,000. When the surgeon shared the outcome with colleagues, they were surprised that such a procedure had been performed at a small centre. For Arpit, this was precisely the kind of change HRS Navigation had hoped to enable: helping skilled doctors access tools that can support complex surgery, even outside the largest hospitals. Another example comes from a trust hospital in Siddhagiri, Maharashtra, where the system has been in use for several years. According to Arpit, patients travel there from Maharashtra and neighbouring Karnataka because the hospital offers treatment at affordable rates. He recalls the case of a mother of three who had a brain tumour in a particularly difficult location. After approaching several larger hospitals, she eventually underwent surgery at the trust hospital. The procedure was successful, and she survived with her neurological functions preserved, Arpit says. Stories such as these illustrate why surgical navigation can matter beyond the operating theatre. When a hospital can offer complex procedures at an affordable cost, patients may have another option closer to home instead of having to travel to a major city. Surgical navigation can help patients access complex procedures closer to home, without travelling to larger cities. The impact is not limited to patients, either. Surgeons can gain confidence from being able to verify their instruments' positions during difficult procedures. Arpit recalls how some senior surgeons initially questioned the system when its guidance differed from their expectations. After repeatedly checking its accuracy during operations, he says many began relying on it as an important part of their workflow. The company also points to a memorable procedure in Guntur in which a patient undergoing brain surgery remained awake and watched the film Baahubali . Unlike most brain surgeries, which are performed under general anaesthesia, an awake craniotomy requires the patient to remain conscious so doctors can monitor essential brain functions in real time. In this case, the patient was comfortable enough to watch a film while the surgical team monitored his responses using HRS Navigation's technology. "The case attracted widespread media attention," Arpit says. For the team, the procedure was a memorable demonstration of how image-guided technology can support surgeons in carefully selected operations where monitoring a patient's core functions is essential. HRS Navigation's systems are now used across a wide range of hospitals, from smaller centres in places such as Guntur and Gorakhpur to larger institutions, including Apollo hospitals and AIIMS facilities. Dr Deshmukh believes such technologies can help narrow the gap between metro and non-metro healthcare facilities, provided hospitals also have the clinical expertise, training and technical support needed to use them effectively. "Advanced surgical technologies should not be limited to a few tertiary centres in major cities," he says. Building medical technology in India, for the world Making precision technology accessible also means rethinking the business model behind it. Arpit says HRS Navigation has avoided recurring consumable costs for every procedure, a model he believes can help hospitals use the system without having to weigh the expense of additional supplies against a patient's ability to pay. The company has also designed easyNav to work with existing operating theatre infrastructure, reducing the need for hospitals to make extensive changes before adopting the technology. These decisions are part of a larger ambition: to demonstrate that sophisticated medical devices can be designed and built in India without compromising on performance. Arpit says HRS Navigation has received international recognition for its product design, including an iF Design Award from Germany and an A' Design Award from Italy. The company has also been selected by India's Department of Science and Technology for recognition linked to the country's 75 years of independence. For him, these milestones matter because medical technology made in India should be judged on what it can achieve, rather than assumptions about where it comes from. "We have taken a long path of doing it from India," he says, describing the company's ambition to become globally respected. That ambition is closely tied to the reason he started the company in the first place. The goal is not only to compete with established international manufacturers but also to make precision healthcare more accessible to people who might otherwise struggle to reach it. HRS Navigation's systems are now installed in over 200 hospitals and have supported more than 20,000 surgeries. Surgical navigation cannot, on its own, solve every challenge in healthcare. The right equipment must work alongside skilled surgeons, trained teams, reliable support and hospitals that patients can afford to access. "But when those pieces come together, technology can expand what a hospital is equipped to offer and give surgeons another tool to make informed decisions," adds Arpit. For the family trying to afford an operation, the surgeon working in a smaller town, or the patient who needs a complex procedure without travelling hundreds of kilometres, that difference can be deeply personal. And that is the promise behind HRS Navigation's homegrown GPS for surgeons: not simply helping doctors find their way through the human body, but helping more patients find their way to advanced surgical care. All images courtesy of HRS Navigation team

items.descriptionOriginal: Sewage is full of organic matter that can be a source of energy. But it also carries harmful chemicals as well as leftover medicines that conventional treatment methods can’t remove easily. Researchers now report a technology that can solve three sewage-related problems at the same time. Their new device uses bacteria in wastewater to generate electricity while breaking down a hard-to-degrade antibiotic and producing a valuable industrial chemical. The team published their results in Journal of Power Sources . There have been plenty of research efforts to harness microbes for treating wastewater while producing renewable energy. The approach uses microbial fuel cells , which are battery-like devices with two electrodes. In microbial fuel cells, bacteria grow on an electrode and devour organic matter , converting chemical energy into electrons, which flow in an external circuit to produce electricity. Then those electrons meet oxygen at the other electrode to create water. Turns out that microbial fuel cells usually generate very small amounts of electricity. “So we asked a different question: What else could those electrons do when they arrive?,” writes the team from both;} Recommended Reading: Designer bacteria clean wastewater and generate power—at the same time If all the electrons don’t combine with oxygen and hydrogen at the second electrode, the product is hydrogen peroxide instead of water. Hydrogen peroxide is a household chemical used for disinfection and bleaching. It is also used widely in chemical manufacturing. The chemical industry makes it today using an energy- and chemical-intensive process in large plants. To get the right reaction in the microbial fuel cell, the researchers designed a new electrode. They embedded iron and nickel oxides on a flexible carbon fiber cloth. When they heated the cloth in the presence of acetylene at 800°C, a forest of carbon nanofibers grew out of it. “The metal particles rode the growing fibers upward, so every fiber ended with a metal oxide tip,” the researchers say. So the electrode has conductive fibers with a catalytic tip. And bacteria cling to this rough conductive surface and form a thick film. The team used the same electrodes on both side of the fuel cell. When they ran sewage spiked with the antibiotic chloramphenicol through the cell, it removed 99.99% of the drug while producing hydrogen peroxide in two days. “Next, we plan to run it longer, test other drugs, check the toxicity of the breakdown products and link several cells in series to raise the power,” the team writes. “So can dirty water help pay for its own cleanup? Not completely yet. But in two days, our system turned sewage into cleaner water, a useful chemical and a little electricity.” Source : Yashmeen Budania et al. In-situ CVD grown FeO & NiO CNF electrode for integrated antibiotic degradation, peroxide production, and bioenergy generation in microbial fuel cells. Journal of Power Sources , 2026. items.descriptionOriginal: In 1995, Professor Sekhar Raghavan noticed something unusual about the water coming from his tap in Chennai. It had turned salty. As groundwater levels fell, seawater was seeping into the city's underground freshwater reserves, making the water increasingly difficult to use. The problem was not that Chennai received too little rain. The city received substantial rainfall, but much of it flowed through roads and drains into the sea instead of replenishing the groundwater beneath its homes. For Raghavan, this raised a question. If the rain was falling over the city, why was so little of it being saved? His answer was to take rainwater harvesting to the people. Armed with a bicycle and a simple message, he began visiting neighbourhoods, going from door to door to convince residents to collect rainwater and direct it back into the ground. Nearly three decades later, his campaign offers a lesson to another Indian city struggling with water scarcity: Hyderabad. When the rain falls, but the wells run dry Home to around 1.5 crore people, the city is grappling with an acute drinking water shortage driven by uneven regional water availability, competing agricultural and industrial demand, and a monsoon deficit. More than 330 of Telangana's 600-plus mandals have been classified as drought-hit, while only around 500 of the state's 6,000-plus lakes have water, according to data shared by the state irrigation department. The pressure is visible in the city's growing dependence on tankers . Daily bookings have surged to between 6,000 and 8,000, prompting Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board Managing Director Ashok Reddy to direct officials to onboard additional tanker operators and begin their registration. In parts of Secunderabad Cantonment and Hyderabad's outskirts, residents have reported receiving drinking water only once every three to four days. One of the city's main reservoirs has also reportedly fallen to around 13% of its capacity. But the shortage is not only about how much water a city receives. It is also about how much it can retain. That is where Chennai's experience becomes relevant. One bicycle, one neighbourhood at a time When Raghavan began his campaign in 1995, rainwater harvesting was not a familiar practice among most urban households. He set out to change that, explaining how rainwater collected from rooftops, driveways and other surfaces could be filtered and directed into recharge structures, allowing it to seep into the soil and replenish underground aquifers. Instead of allowing rainwater to run off into drains, households could capture it and help restore the groundwater they depended on. However, convincing people was harder than explaining the science. Raghavan cycled through neighbourhoods, speaking to residents and encouraging them to install harvesting systems. Many initially dismissed the idea, but he continued working with communities to demonstrate how it could be done. Through the Rain Centre, which he led, he also worked with a team of plumbers and well-diggers to survey systems across the city and demonstrate rainwater harvesting through model houses. How Chennai turned an idea into a law In October 2002, the Tamil Nadu government enacted legislation to make rainwater harvesting compulsory. An ordinance followed in June 2003, extending the requirement to all existing buildings across the state, including Chennai. Property owners were required to install systems by 11 October, 2003. Non-compliance could invite penalties, including fines or disconnection of government water supply. The government's November 2003 announcement reported that 99.5% of Chennai's residents had implemented rainwater harvesting in their houses and apartment complexes. But installing a system and making it work are two different things. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) A Rain Centre survey conducted in a residential colony between October and November 2003 found that around half the residents had implemented rainwater harvesting unsatisfactorily. Even among those who had installed systems correctly, many focused only on collecting rooftop rainwater. They overlooked another important source: the rain falling across the rest of their premises. In apartment complexes, this surface runoff could amount to twice or more the volume collected from rooftops. Although this water may not be suitable for direct household use, it can still be directed into the soil to replenish groundwater. As it moves through the soil, natural filtration helps remove contaminants. The missing piece: What happens beyond the rooftop? Raghavan's work also highlighted a larger gap in Chennai's approach. While households had a responsibility to harvest rainwater within their properties, public spaces presented another opportunity. Roads, parks and playgrounds receive considerable rainfall. Yet much of the water flowing through Chennai's stormwater drains is channelled towards the city's waterwys and eventually discharged into the Bay of Bengal. Instead of allowing all this runoff to escape, the Rain Centre advocated directing suitable urban runoff into recharge structures. This, however, requires careful planning. Road runoff carries solid waste, fine silt and other contaminants that can clog harvesting structures. Systems must therefore account for filtration, waste removal and regular maintenance. In parts of Secunderabad Cantonment and Hyderabad's outskirts, residents have reported receiving drinking water only once every three to four days. Photograph: (Representational image-Aijaz Rahi/AP Photo) The city also needs adequate open spaces and appropriately designed recharge structures to prevent stagnant water and flooding. In other words, collecting rainwater is only one part of managing it. What Chennai's experience tells Hyderabad The results of Chennai's efforts became more visible after the rains returned. Tamil Nadu received below-average rainfall in 2003 and 2004, making the immediate benefits difficult for residents to see. The following year brought heavier rainfall, offering a clearer demonstration of what functioning harvesting systems could achieve. After the 2005 rains, the Rain Centre observed groundwater levels rising by around 20 feet in areas it monitored, encouraging the team to continue its work. For nearly 15 years, rainwater harvesting helped Chennai strengthen its groundwater reserves . However, the city's 2019 water crisis exposed the limitations of relying on infrastructure that was no longer adequately maintained. Clogged filters, neglected recharge pits, and poorly functioning systems weakened the impact of the original initiative. Today, Chennai is exploring additional approaches, including sponge parks and underground rainwater capture systems, to improve its capacity to retain rainfall. For Hyderabad, the lesson is not simply to replicate Chennai's legislation or install harvesting structures across buildings . It is to build a system in which households, communities and civic authorities share responsibility for capturing rainwater, maintaining recharge structures and protecting groundwater. Raghavan's journey began with a salty tap and a bicycle. What followed was a citywide conversation that helped turn an overlooked resource into an urban water-management priority. Sources: 'Can storm water drains help in recharging groundwater: The case of Chennai' : By India Water Portal team, Published on 22 November 2014 'Hyderabad in the grips of severe drinking water crisis—8,000 tankers a day, supply once in 3 days' : By Deepika Amirapu, Published on 24 October, 2026 'Chennai Water Crisis: 71-YO 'Rain Man' Helps Hundreds Recharge Their Groundwater' : By Tanvi Patel, Published on 29 Jun 2019
