items.descriptionOriginal: On 5 November, Delhi's Air Quality Index (AQI) reached 370 , placing the capital in the very poor category. At Jahangirpuri, the reading climbed to 459, entering the severe category. As winter settles over northern India, the familiar response is to increase road sweeping, sprinkle water and intensify construction-site inspections. Yet there is a problem with the way cities clean their roads. A street can look spotless while fine particles escape into the air. Vehicles can then lift the remaining dust again, exposing pedestrians, cyclists and residents to pollution. The question is not simply whether municipalities should sweep more often, but whether they can remove dust without making it airborne. Three Indian cities offer different answers . Lucknow has expanded mechanised sweeping, Parwanoo has focused on repairing the surfaces that generate dust, and Chandigarh is testing a method that combines treated-water washing with mechanical cleaning. Together, their experiences show why cleaner roads require more than a broom. Lucknow takes cleaning beyond the broom In September 2026, Lucknow won the top position in the Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan among cities with populations exceeding 10 lakh. Its Ward 70, in Zone 4, also ranked first nationally among wards with more than 30,000 residents. The recognition followed a citywide effort to tackle several sources of pollution, including road dust, vehicle emissions and waste burning. Loose soil and debris along road shoulders can be repeatedly disturbed by traffic, making roadside maintenance an important part of dust control. Photograph: ( Hindustan Times ) The Lucknow Municipal Corporation deployed 97 electric mechanised sweeping machines. These machines use rotating brushes to collect debris, while suction systems can help capture finer material instead of simply pushing it aside. The city also paved approximately 559.85 km of roads end-to-end, reducing exposed surfaces that passing vehicles can disturb. Officials said the combination of mechanised sweeping and paving helped control resuspended road dust. The ward-level recognition is particularly significant because air pollution is experienced locally. A city may have an ambitious clean-air plan , but residents encounter its results on the street outside their homes. Ward 70's achievement shows how clean-air action can be assessed at a neighbourhood level. However, the award does not establish how much pollution the ward's individual interventions reduced. The challenge is to translate recognition into sustained, measurable improvements in the air residents breathe. Parwanoo fixes the road that creates the dust In Parwanoo, a town in Himachal Pradesh, officials began by asking a different question: what if the road itself was generating the dust? Damaged road surfaces, crumbling edges and poorly managed construction waste can all contribute to the dust that settles on urban streets. Photograph: ( TOI ) An IIT Kanpur study covering the town's 8.5 sq km identified road dust as a major source of air pollution . The municipal response focused on repairing the surfaces and conditions that allowed dust to accumulate. A 9 km stretch of road was upgraded with paver blocks and interlocking tiles, replacing crumbling surfaces. Drainage systems were improved to prevent erosion, while construction and demolition waste came under closer scrutiny. The town also developed a 0.27-acre green buffer zone, intensified plantation efforts, and curbed open garbage dumping. The outcome was measurable. Parwanoo's annual average PM10 concentration fell from 66 micrograms per cubic metre in 2017-18 to 39 micrograms per cubic metre in 2023-24, a reduction of about 41%. PM10 refers to particles with a diameter of 10 micrometres or less. Road dust can contain these particles, which can enter the respiratory system. The reduction cannot be attributed to paving alone. Parwanoo's efforts included several interventions, and the town's experience demonstrates the value of addressing dust at its source rather than relying exclusively on cleaning after it has accumulated. Chandigarh tests whether washing can help Chandigarh is approaching the problem through a pilot project. In September 2025, the Chandigarh Pollution Control Committee directed officials to launch a dust-control initiative on a dust-prone road corridor. The plan combined road washing with treated water, mechanised sweeping and cleaning of road shoulders. Road dust contains PM10 particles, which measure 10 micrometres or less in diameter and can enter the respiratory system. Photograph: ( HT ) Road shoulders matter because loose soil and debris along the edges can be repeatedly disturbed by vehicles. Cleaning only the central carriageway can leave a substantial source of dust untouched. The committee planned to monitor PM10 levels during the pilot and use the findings to decide whether the intervention could be expanded across the city. The project also sits within a wider effort to control construction and demolition waste. Authorities directed institutions and agencies to suppress dust at stockyards, cover loose soil with vegetation and use sprinklers or anti-smog guns where appropriate. The distinction is important: Chandigarh's project was announced as a pilot, not a proven citywide success. Its value lies in testing whether road washing and mechanical cleaning can work together, and whether air-quality monitoring can establish their effectiveness. What Delhi can learn Delhi's pollution is not caused by road dust alone. Vehicle emissions, industrial activity, construction, waste burning, agricultural fires and winter weather conditions all contribute to the city's air-quality episodes. But that does not make road dust control insignificant. It makes targeted interventions more important. Lucknow demonstrates the value of mechanised cleaning and neighbourhood-level action. Parwanoo shows why repairing damaged roads and controlling construction waste can prevent dust from accumulating. Chandigarh is testing whether treated-water washing and shoulder cleaning can improve the results. The larger lesson is that road cleaning should not be measured only by the amount of dust collected or the number of machines deployed. Road dust control works best when cities prevent loose particles from returning to the air, making cleaner streets a practical step towards healthier urban environments. Photograph: ( The Indian Express ) Municipalities need to measure how much dust remains on roads, how quickly it returns, and whether particulate pollution declines. For a city like Delhi, where winter pollution can become a public-health emergency, cleaner roads are not a complete solution. But they are a tangible civic intervention that can be planned, monitored, and improved. The real test of a clean road is not how it looks after a sweeping vehicle passes. It is how much dust stays out of the air afterwards. Sources ' Lucknow is known for traffic and dust. How did it top India's clean-air ranking? items.descriptionOriginal: Η επαγγελματική έκθεση σε λιπαντικά που προέρχονται από το πετρέλαιο, όπως το λάδι κινητήρα, το υδραυλικό λάδι και τα υγρά κοπής που χρησιμοποιούνται για την ψύξη ή τη λίπανση μετάλλων κατά την κατεργασία τους, συνδέεται με αυξημένες πιθανότητες εμφάνισης Σκλήρυνσης κατά Πλάκας (ΣΚΠ), σύμφωνα με μελέτη που δημοσιεύθηκε στο επιστημονικό περιοδικό «Neurology» της Αμερικανικής Ακαδημίας Νευρολογίας. Στη ΣΚΠ το ανοσοποιητικό σύστημα επιτίθεται στον εγκέφαλο, τον νωτιαίο μυελό και τα οπτικά νεύρα. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Protecting Forests from Disturbance Outperforms Restoration for Amazon Biodiversity, Study Finds Reading Time: 3 minutes Across 3 million hectares of the Brazilian Amazon, protecting forests from disturbance delivered greater biodiversity benefits than restoring already-cleared land, according to new research comparing conservation strategies. Conservation policy has long debated where limited funding should go: preventing deforestation outright, protecting standing forests from degradation, or restoring land already cleared. A study published in Science this September provides the clearest answer yet, using counterfactual scenarios built from observed land-use changes across three million hectares of the Brazilian Amazon’s deforestation frontier. Led by Leonardo S. Miranda of Lancaster University alongside researchers including Joice Ferreira of Embrapa, the team compared three intervention types against what actually happened on the ground. Protecting forests from disturbance, meaning avoiding fire and selective logging within standing forest, reduced biodiversity loss by 68.5% and carbon loss by 46.8% compared with the baseline scenario. Avoiding deforestation entirely mitigated 60.8% of carbon loss and 28.0% of biodiversity loss. Restoration of already-cleared land delivered the smallest gains for both outcomes. These findings challenge a common assumption in conservation funding, where restoration often receives outsized attention and investment despite standing forests requiring protection first. Protecting forests from disturbance proved nearly as effective as preventing deforestation for carbon storage, while substantially outperforming it for biodiversity outcomes, a distinction with direct implications for how governments and conservation organizations allocate resources. Neither single intervention alone reversed losses across the landscape. Combining avoided deforestation with protection from disturbance was necessary to achieve net-positive outcomes, increasing biodiversity by 12% and carbon by 18% above 2010 baseline levels. This combined approach proved essential precisely because deforestation and forest degradation operate through different mechanisms, requiring complementary rather than substitutable responses. Restoration still carries genuine value, particularly in landscapes where deforestation has already progressed extensively. The research team found that restoration delivered meaningful benefits, particularly on properties where much of the original forest cover had already disappeared, suggesting it works best as a complement to protection rather than a replacement. Protecting forests from disturbance addresses threats that often receive less policy attention than outright deforestation. Selective logging removes valuable timber species while leaving forest canopy nominally intact, and wildfires increasingly penetrate forest edges weakened by fragmentation and drought. Both processes degrade forest structure, reduce habitat quality for forest-dependent species, and release stored carbon, yet they generate far less public attention than visible clear-cutting. Protecting forests from disturbance targets fire and selective logging, threats that degrade forest structure without clear-cutting, with researchers finding that combined deforestation and disturbance avoidance are necessary to achieve net-positive biodiversity and carbon outcomes above 2010 baseline levels. Photo by Bill Salazar on Pexels. The study’s timing is especially urgent as climate change intensifies. The research team noted that combined interventions become increasingly important as warming progresses, since forest restoration efforts prove particularly vulnerable to wildfire risk. Newly planted or naturally regenerating young forests lack the structural resilience of mature canopies, making restoration investments vulnerable to being undone by the same fire disturbances the study identifies as critical to prevent. This vulnerability creates a policy challenge extending well beyond Brazil. As governments and international organizations increasingly emphasize forest restoration within climate commitments and biodiversity frameworks, protecting forests from disturbance offers a complementary message: restoration investments achieve far less impact when the remaining standing forest around them continues degrading from fire and logging. Joice Ferreira, principal investigator of the Capoeira restoration research program at Embrapa, emphasized that restoration remains essential precisely where forests have been lost across large areas, reinforcing that the study’s findings don’t diminish restoration’s role but rather clarify where and when it delivers the strongest returns. Restoration works best as part of integrated strategies rather than as a primary tool used independently of forest protection efforts. The research methodology itself offers a template for conservation planning elsewhere. By using observed land-use changes to construct counterfactual scenarios, the team measured what would have happened under different intervention choices and quantified trade-offs that previous studies could only estimate qualitatively. This approach allows policymakers to weigh cost-effectiveness directly rather than relying on intuition about which conservation strategy delivers the greatest return per dollar invested. As tropical deforestation frontiers worldwide face similar pressures from fire, logging, and agricultural expansion, protecting forests from disturbance provides an evidence-based framework extending beyond the Brazilian Amazon alone. The findings suggest that conservation funding achieves maximum impact not through any single strategy in isolation, but through carefully sequenced combinations addressing deforestation, degradation, and restoration simultaneously, each targeting the specific threats most relevant to a given landscape’s current condition. The post Protecting Forests from Disturbance Outperforms Restoration for Amazon Biodiversity, Study Finds appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Every Diwali, the night sky turns into a canvas of colour. Golden fountains of light shoot upwards, flower pots scatter sparkling trails across balconies, and rockets burst into brilliant shades of red, green and blue. For a few hours, the neighbourhood seems to glow with celebration. But when the last spark fades, another side of the festivities begins to show. A cloud of smoke hangs over the streets, the familiar smell of burnt chemicals lingers in the air, and the sound of crackers gives way to coughing, irritated eyes, and difficulty breathing. Firecrackers may last only a few seconds, but the pollution they leave behind can stay in the air much longer. This has led to the growing popularity of an alternative: green crackers. But are they actually better for the environment, and does the word 'green' mean they are safe to burst? What happens when a firecracker goes off? The colourful explosions we enjoy are the result of carefully mixed chemicals that release energy when ignited. But this reaction also releases a cocktail of pollutants into the atmosphere. Conventional firecrackers can emit particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and other harmful gases. These tiny particles can enter the respiratory system, with some travelling deep into the lungs and even entering the bloodstream. For people with asthma , respiratory conditions or heart problems, exposure can make existing symptoms worse. Children and older adults are particularly vulnerable. Even otherwise healthy people may experience coughing, throat irritation, breathlessness and burning eyes. Green crackers use modified chemical formulations designed to reduce particulate emissions compared with conventional fireworks. Photograph: ( Khan Global studies ) There is also the problem of noise pollution. The sudden, loud bursts can cause distress to infants, older people, pets and those sensitive to sound. And when thousands of crackers are burst across a city within a few hours, their emissions add to the pollution already coming from vehicles, industries and other sources. What makes a firecracker green? To address this problem, scientists at the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), along with the National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI), developed what are known as green crackers. Introduced in India in 2019, these are firecrackers made with modified chemical formulations and reduced quantities of certain raw materials. The idea is simple: retain the familiar sparkle and sound of fireworks while releasing fewer pollutants. Developed by CSIR and NEERI, green crackers fall into three categories: SWAS, STAR and SAFAL, each using a different approach to reduce emissions. Photograph: ( GCESCJ ) According to NEERI's criteria, a green cracker must reduce particulate matter emissions by at least 30% compared with its conventional counterpart. Another qualifying formulation must achieve at least 20% lower particulate emissions, along with a minimum 10% reduction in gaseous emissions such as sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide. The chemistry behind the sparkle So, what actually changes inside these crackers? Scientists work on changing the ingredients, reducing the amount of material used, and making combustion more efficient. There are three recognised categories: SWAS (Safe Water Releaser): These crackers release water vapour during combustion, which helps suppress dust particles and reduce particulate emissions. STAR (Safe Thermite Cracker): These use iron oxide-based formulations to improve combustion efficiency and reduce emissions. SAFAL (Safe Minimal Aluminium): These use zeolite-based materials, which have a porous structure, to help reduce the amount of aluminium required. Green crackers also exclude certain harmful chemicals, including barium nitrate, and use modified formulations to reduce ash and other emissions. Are green crackers completely safe? Here's where the distinction matters: less polluting does not mean pollution-free. Even green crackers release particulate matter and gases when burnt. Some green crackers could release higher numbers of ultrafine particles than conventional ones. These extremely tiny particles are concerning because they can penetrate deep into the respiratory system. This does not mean every green cracker is more harmful, but it shows why simply measuring the total quantity of emissions does not tell the whole story. There is another important point. A 30% reduction in emissions from an individual cracker does not mean the air in a city becomes 30% cleaner. The overall impact depends on how many crackers are burst, the pollutants they release, weather conditions, and other sources of pollution. Green crackers, therefore, are a step towards reducing the damage, not a licence to burst as many as we like. Choosing fewer firecrackers and exploring alternative ways to celebrate can help reduce Diwali's impact on the air we breathe. Photograph: ( The Indian Express ) If buying them, look for products from authorised manufacturers with valid certification rather than trusting packaging that simply says 'eco-friendly' or 'pollution-free' . Perhaps the best way to make Diwali brighter is to think beyond the few seconds a firecracker lights up the sky. Green crackers offer a way to reduce some of the harm, but they cannot take pollution out of the picture entirely. Choosing to burst fewer crackers, exploring other ways to celebrate, and being mindful of the air we all share can make a difference. After all, a festival of lights should leave behind happy memories, not air that makes it harder for people to breathe. Sources: 'Green firecrackers may pollute less, but how clean are they? An expert explains' by Hina Rohtaki for The Indian Express, Published on 31 October 2026. 'EXPLAINED | Green Crackers Allowed for Diwali: What Does 'Green' Really Mean?' by Sunny KS for Open The Magazine

items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine walking through the Western Ghats after the monsoon. The soil is damp, leaves glisten with rain, and tiny saplings grow in the shade of towering trees. Each tree seems to live a life of its own, reaching towards sunlight. Yet beneath your feet, another world is at work. Tiny fungal threads spread through the soil, forming partnerships with tree roots. They help trees find water and nutrients, while the trees provide them with food. Some fungal threads may even connect neighbouring plants. This hidden world has earned a nickname: the 'wood wide web'. But can trees really share resources through it? And what might these underground relationships tell us about protecting forests? The surprising give-and-take beneath tree roots Trees use sunlight to make sugars through photosynthesis. But getting essential nutrients from the ground is another matter. That is where fungi come in. Their microscopic threads reach into tiny spaces in the soil that tree roots cannot easily explore. They help plants take up nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen, and can also improve access to water. In exchange, trees supply the fungi with carbon-rich sugars. Scientists call these partnerships mycorrhizal associations . The name may be unfamiliar, but the arrangement is simple. The fungal threads, known as hyphae , can spread through soil to form a larger web called mycelium . Some fungi associate with several plants at once, potentially linking their roots in what researchers call common mycorrhizal networks . The links are intriguing. What is less certain is whether they regularly allow one tree to support another. Fungi extend through the soil as microscopic filaments called hyphae. Collectively, these filaments form a network known as mycelium. Photograph: (Kabir Gabriel Peay; Advanced Science News) How scientists began mapping the wood wide web In 2019, an international team of researchers, including scientists from Stanford University and ETH Zurich, set out to understand where different tree-fungus partnerships occur around the world. They analysed records from more than 1.1 million forest plots across over 70 countries, covering upwards of 28,000 tree species. With the help of computer models, they mapped the distribution of major types of tree-root partnerships, including those involving fungi and nitrogen-fixing bacteria. The study, published in Nature , showed that these relationships vary with climate. In cooler regions, for instance, the way dead leaves and other organic matter break down can influence which fungal partners thrive. The findings revealed global patterns beneath the forest floor. They also raised questions about how changes in temperature and rainfall could affect the partnerships on which trees depend. Importantly, the scientists mapped broad patterns of association. They did not trace individual fungal threads linking particular trees. Do older trees help younger ones? Perhaps the most captivating idea linked to the wood wide web is that of a 'mother tree': a large, older tree that nourishes nearby seedlings through shared fungal connections. Picture a tiny sapling struggling for sunlight beneath a thick forest canopy. Studies have found that materials can sometimes move between plants associated with fungal networks. But observing movement does not automatically show that a mature tree deliberately helps a seedling, or that the transfer makes the younger tree healthier. In 2023, researchers reviewed studies of common mycorrhizal networks in Nature Ecology & Evolution . They warned that some popular claims had travelled further than the evidence. In particular, they found no published peer-reviewed evidence that mature trees preferentially send resources or warning signals to their own offspring through these networks. So the underground partnerships are real. The popular picture of forests acting like families that look after one another remains unproven. What happens when forest soil is disturbed? Think of the rainforests of the Western Ghats, the sal forests of central and eastern India, or the mountain forests of the Himalayas. Their climates, soils and trees differ, and so do the organisms living around their roots. The 2019 global study offers clues about where different partnerships might occur. It cannot tell us exactly which trees are connected beneath any particular Indian forest. That is why studying local soils and fungi matters. Forest health depends on far more than what grows above ground. Underground organisms help trees obtain nutrients, support the recycling of organic matter and influence how plants respond to changing conditions. When forests are cleared or soils disturbed, these relationships can be disrupted too. Understanding them could help scientists think more carefully about restoring degraded land and protecting existing forests. The next time you walk among trees, consider the soil beneath them. Hidden there are thousands of living connections, doing essential work even as scientists continue to uncover how they function. Protecting a forest begins with understanding the life we can see, and the life we cannot. Source: 'Stanford researchers map symbiotic relationships between trees and microbes worldwide' : By Stanford Report, Published on 15 May 2019 'Mycorrhizal feedbacks influence global forest structure and diversity' : Published on 19 October 2023

items.descriptionOriginal: For centuries, the sacred groves of Rajasthan were understood as human gifts to nature -- places where belief drew a boundary and the forest was allowed to breathe. But as this essay quietly argues, the order of that story is wrong: people protected a handful of fig trees, and the birds did everything else. The peepal, the banyan, the gular -- three figs that tradition placed beyond the reach of the axe - fed birds through every lean season, and those birds, carrying seeds from across the landscape, built the grove outward from that protected center, generation after generation. "What belief really preserved was a process," the author writes, "a place where the planting could go on undisturbed for centuries." There is something worth sitting with in that realization: that the deepest acts of protection are often for something we cannot fully see, and that what looks like a tree standing alone is, if the birds still come, a forest in the making.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Forest Landscape Restoration in Mozambique Launches in Nampula Province Reading Time: 3 minutes Forest landscape restoration in Mozambique has officially begun in Nampula Province, aiming to restore 500 hectares of Miombo woodland and build local livelihoods. Forest landscape restoration in Mozambique took a major step forward this August with the official launch of a new project in Nampula Province. The initiative pairs the Mozambican government with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), funded by Swiss Development Cooperation. Its goal is to turn national restoration pledges into work that communities can see on the ground. The launch unfolded over two days in Ribáuè District, starting with a briefing for provincial officials and continuing with a public ceremony. Government representatives, private companies, researchers, and local residents participated. Seedlings planted during the event were handed over to a nearby school, where students will track their growth. IUCN’s country representative in Mozambique described the project as reaching well beyond tree planting. The effort aims to improve land productivity and strengthen household livelihoods alongside ecological recovery. That framing positions forest landscape restoration in Mozambique as much an economic strategy as an environmental one. Over the next four years, the project will focus restoration work on 500 hectares within Ribáuè District. Of that total, 400 hectares will restore Miombo woodland, while the remaining 100 hectares will support agroforestry systems mixing crops with trees. The work contributes to Mozambique’s broader Five-Year Programme target of restoring 52,000 hectares nationwide. That national target also feeds into Mozambique’s international commitments under global restoration initiatives. Countries across Africa have pledged millions of hectares to these efforts over the past decade, though turning pledges into on-the-ground results has often proven difficult. A dedicated project with clear hectare targets and funding attached is meant to help close that gap. Miombo woodland stretches across a huge swath of south-central Africa, from Angola to Tanzania and across much of Mozambique. The ecosystem stores significant amounts of carbon and supports roughly half of Africa’s remaining elephant population. Millions of rural households also depend on it directly for firewood, food, and building materials. That dependence cuts both ways. Wood fuel accounts for a large share of household energy use across the Miombo region, which keeps pressure on the woodland high even where restoration work is underway. Providing communities with alternative income sources, rather than relying solely on wood and charcoal, is central to keeping any restored area intact over the long term. Alongside the restoration targets, the project will establish three plant nurseries to supply seedlings for ongoing work. Planners also intend to develop beekeeping and support sustainable value chains tied to cashew, bamboo, and legally harvested timber. Those activities aim to give residents income tied directly to keeping the landscape intact, a key piece of how forest landscape restoration in Mozambique is meant to work in practice. Forest landscape restoration in Mozambique ties livelihood directly to conservation, with three community nurseries, beekeeping, and sustainable value chains for cashew, bamboo, and timber giving Nampula residents concrete economic reasons to keep the landscape intact. Photo courtesy of IUCN . Mozambique’s project forms part of a larger global effort known as the FLR Hub, implemented by IUCN alongside other international partners. The hub originally supported restoration work across six countries in Africa and Latin America. A new contribution from Switzerland, announced in late 2025, extended that reach to Mozambique, bringing the total to seven participating countries. According to IUCN, the hub aims to shift restoration efforts from scattered, one-off projects to coordinated approaches that attract long-term investment. That shift matters for a landscape as large and fragmented as the Miombo, where piecemeal efforts have struggled to keep pace with ongoing degradation. Implementation in Ribáuè will rely on continued collaboration between government agencies, private businesses, universities, and civil society groups. Success will depend on whether restored land can deliver real income for residents, not just healthier soil and more trees. Four years is a short window to prove that the model works, but it gives the project a clear point at which results can be measured against the hectare targets set at launch. If it works, forest landscape restoration in Mozambique could offer a model other Miombo countries draw on as they pursue their own restoration commitments. The post Forest Landscape Restoration in Mozambique Launches in Nampula Province appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: The next time you pick up a notebook, pause for a moment. An earthy brown cover , a leaf logo, or the words 'eco-friendly' might make it look like the greener choice. But appearances can be deceptive. What you should consider is the paper inside, the materials used to make it, how long it lasts, and whether it can be recycled after use. For Ashutosh Ananth, co-founder of paper and stationery brand 'Rescript' , sustainability is about looking beyond appearances and rethinking how everyday paper products are made. "A notebook being sustainable is about much more than having a kraft cover or looking natural. You have to look at what it is made from, how it is put together, how long it will last, and what happens to it after you are done using it," he says. Founded in 2021 by Ashutosh and his school friend Naren Raj, the brand makes copier paper, notebooks, journals, planners, and other stationery using 100 percent recycled paper. After pursuing ideas such as biofuels in 2019, the friends entered corporate gifting. That experience showed them how much paper businesses consume every day. "We realised that the opportunity was much larger than gifting. If we could make everyday paper products more sustainable, the impact could be greater," he says. Recycled paper and notebooks became their starting point, eventually growing into a wider stationery range. So, what should you look for when buying a notebook? The co-founder shares six things consumers should check before making a choice. 1. Check what the paper is made from Since paper makes up most of a notebook, its composition is the first thing to examine. Rather than relying on broad descriptions such as 'eco-friendly', 'green' or 'sustainable', he recommends looking for a clear statement of the recycled content. Founded in 2021 by Ashutosh and his school friend Naren Raj, the brand makes copier paper, notebooks, journals, planners, and other stationery using 100 percent recycled paper. "A notebook made with 100 percent recycled paper reduces the need for virgin fibre and gives already-used paper another life," he explains. The percentage matters. A notebook containing 10 or 20 percent recycled fibre is different from one made entirely from recycled paper, even though both may be marketed as containing recycled material. If virgin fibre is used, consumers should also look for information about whether it is responsibly sourced. "Look at the fibre composition, including how much is recycled and where any virgin fibre comes from," he adds. 2. Look for credible certifications Claims are more meaningful when independently verified. Ashutosh recommends checking recognised labels such as the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) and the Programme for the Endorsement of Forest Certification (PEFC), while understanding what each means. An FSC Recycled label verifies that the relevant fibre is 100 percent recycled. FSC Mix, on the other hand, can include a combination of recycled material, FSC-certified virgin fibre and controlled virgin fibre. "A precisely stated fibre composition, certification number, and manufacturing information tell you much more than a brown cover with a leaf printed on it," he says. 3. Do not judge the paper by its colour Brown, beige, and grey paper are mostly associated with sustainability. But a notebook's colour alone cannot tell you how responsibly it has been made. "A brownish or grey notebook does not necessarily mean it is more sustainable," he says. "Colour can tell you something about how the paper has been processed, but it does not tell you enough about where the fibre came from, how much of it is recycled, or how responsibly the notebook has been made." Bright white paper may undergo additional processing, bleaching, and optical brightening. Recycled paper can also be made bright white, while virgin paper can be brown or beige. "Rescript uses careful sourcing, segregation, de-inking, and controlled processing, while avoiding chlorine bleaching, to achieve its natural warm-white shade. For us, the goal was never just to make recycled paper. It was to make recycled paper that people would choose because it is good paper," he explains. 4. Examine the cover and finishing A notebook may contain recycled paper but still include materials that make it harder to recycle. Plastic lamination, synthetic covers, heavy coatings, foil, and other decorative finishes can add to the number of materials used. When these are permanently bonded to paper, separating them at the end of the notebook's life can become more difficult. Recycled paper and notebooks became their starting point, eventually growing into a wider stationery range. "It is common to talk about sustainable paper while adding heavily laminated, plastic-coated or synthetic covers around it," he says. He recommends paper-based or recycled covers and avoiding finishes that serve little practical purpose. 5. Make sure it is built to last Sustainability is not only about what a notebook is made from. It is also about how long it remains useful. A notebook with weak pages, poor binding, or a cover that falls apart prematurely may need to be replaced before it has served its purpose. "A notebook that falls apart halfway through its life and has to be replaced is not particularly sustainable," the co-founder says. Check the binding, paper strength, and construction. Thread binding keeps materials relatively simple, while a metal spiral can usually be separated from the paper before recycling. "Choosing to stay sustainable should not mean accepting an inferior product," he says. "The ideal is to get both things right. A lower-impact material and a genuinely good product made from it." 6. Consider what happens after the last page Ashutosh recommends choosing products with easier construction and fewer unnecessary non-paper components. Once a notebook has been completely used, removable metal spirals and other separable parts should be taken off where possible. Plastic lamination, glitter, foil, and heavy coatings deserve particular attention because some can interfere with the recovery of paper fibres. Recyclability also depends on the facilities available locally, so consumers should check what their local recycler accepts. "The less the construction, the easier it generally is to recover and recycle the materials," he says. His advice is to use the notebook fully, separate removable components, keep the paper clean and dry, and check local guidance. "Recyclability is not just about whether a material can theoretically be recycled somewhere in the world. It is about whether the product has been designed sensibly enough, and whether the recycling system available to you can actually recover it," he explains. Turning recycled paper into an everyday choice For Ashutosh and Naren, these considerations are central to Rescript's effort to make recycled paper a common choice for consumers and businesses. Their paper is made from 100 percent recycled material and processed without chlorine bleaching. Its published comparisons state that the paper uses around 50 percent less water and produces 37 percent lower carbon dioxide emissions than its conventional paper benchmark. The company holds FSC certification under licence code FSC C163185. Since paper makes up most of a notebook, its composition is the first thing to examine. As of September 2026, it has used more than 1,000 tonnes of recycled paper since its launch. The company estimates that this represents more than 18,000 trees saved, around four crore litres of water conserved and approximately 13 lakh kilograms of carbon dioxide emissions avoided compared with producing an equivalent quantity through conventional virgin-paper processes. It now supplies products to individual customers as well as institutional and corporate buyers, including DMart, JP Morgan, Hero MotoCorp, LIC, and ICICI Prudential. Ashutosh says replacing conventional paper at scale can accelerate the impact. "We use recycled paper because we believe it is the right material choice, but the ambition is not only to make a sustainable notebook. It is to make a notebook that someone would choose for its paper, texture, construction, and experience even if sustainability were not the first thing on their mind," he concludes. All pictures courtesy Rescript.

items.titleOriginal: Personalized brain therapy hits 68 percent remission for PTSD
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ ΑΙΣΙΟΔΟΞΟΥ Μια νέα θεραπεία που εγκρίθηκε από τον FDA για το PTSD ανέφερε ύφεση 68 τοις εκατό σε κλινικές δοκιμές. Η θεραπεία, που ονομάζεται Μαγνητική e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), αναπτύχθηκε από την Wave Neuroscience με έδρα την Καλιφόρνια σε συνεργασία με…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A newly FDA-cleared treatment for PTSD reported 68 percent remission in clinical trials. The best-performing approved medications for the condition top out at around 10.9 percent. The treatment, called Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), was developed by California-based Wave Neuroscience in collaboration with researchers at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology. It pairs brain activity mapping with personalized magnetic stimulation. The clinical trial also reported a 52 percent reduction in PTSD symptoms overall. “Our FDA trial reported a 52 percent reduction in symptoms, so more than a four-fold increase in efficacy,” said Erik Won, D.O., Wave Neuroscience’s chief medical officer. “And more importantly, we saw 68 percent remission in our clinical trial. From a clinical care perspective, that’s really meaningful.” These results come from different studies, not a direct head-to-head comparison, but the gap is hard to ignore. How MeRT personalizes treatment The process starts with an electroencephalogram (EEG) that records each patient’s brain electrical activity. An AI-assisted algorithm uses that data to build a personalized stimulation plan. A coil placed against the scalp then delivers targeted magnetic pulses through transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), a technique already FDA-cleared for treatment-resistant depression . Standard TMS follows a generalized protocol. MeRT adjusts based on what’s happening in each patient’s brain. Dr. Kenneth S. Ramos, a precision medicine researcher at Texas A&M Health who helped guide the study, put it this way: standard TMS covers the leak with a tarp; MeRT tries to find and replace the damaged shingles. Participants received five sessions per week over five to six weeks, but improvements appeared to persist after the sessions ended. The first FDA-cleared non-drug option for PTSD PTSD was formally recognized as a diagnosis in 1980 . Since then, treatment has relied on two FDA-approved medications, both SSRIs, and psychotherapy. A 2020 review found medication remission rates reached 10.9 percent at most. MeRT will be the first FDA-cleared non-medication treatment specifically for PTSD. Dr. Israel Liberzon, the study’s lead psychiatrist and a distinguished professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at the Texas A&M Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine, explained what that means for patients. “Right now, the FDA has approved only two medications for PTSD,” he said. “This is the first time that in addition to the medication, we have a non-medication option. There is psychotherapy that people use for PTSD, but psychotherapies require a lot of effort. People must participate actively, and many drop out because it’s too anxiety-provoking. So now we have a unique alternative.” About six percent of Americans will experience PTSD during their lifetime, with higher rates among women and veterans . In the United States, approximately 17.5 veterans die by suicide each day. “People living with PTSD have been left with trial-and-error treatment, medications and their side effects, and limited outcomes—even when treated by the most dedicated and experienced physicians,” Won said. “Wave’s FDA clearance signals a fundamentally different future: one in which PTSD can be objectively evaluated, precisely treated and meaningfully healed.” Wave Neuroscience and Texas A&M Health are working on insurance coverage to make the therapy more widely accessible. Won also believes MeRT could eventually be adapted for depression, anxiety, and other psychiatric conditions. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Personalized brain therapy hits 68 percent remission for PTSD first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Chances are, you’ve got a tube of toothpaste in your bathroom right now. If it’s only going on your teeth, you’re leaving a surprisingly useful cleaning tool sitting on your bathroom counter. Joy Ramos , a professional cleaner and operations manager at Bear Bros Cleaning, has long used toothpaste for jobs well beyond the bathroom. Most white, non-gel toothpastes contain mild abrasive particles that work like ultra-fine sandpaper, polishing surfaces without scratching them. It turns out that property has a lot of household uses. One thing before you start: plain white, non-gel toothpaste is what you want. Gel formulas don’t have the same abrasive particles, and heavily whitening varieties can be too harsh on delicate surfaces. Always rinse thoroughly after using it, and when in doubt, test on a discreet spot first. For scratches and cloudy surfaces A light scratch on glass (a phone screen, a coffee table, a mirror) can often be buffed out with a small amount of toothpaste on a microfiber cloth. Work in gentle circles, then wipe clean. The abrasives smooth the area around the scratch rather than filling it, so it becomes much less visible. The same trick works on fogged car headlights. Rub toothpaste over the lens in small circular motions for a minute or two, then rinse and dry. Repeat if needed. Wood is another one. Water rings and minor scratches on countertops or floors respond well to a small amount applied with a soft cloth. Follow the grain, wipe off, and dry thoroughly. For metals and fixtures Hard water takes the shine out of faucets and handles over time. Toothpaste can bring it back on stainless steel and chrome, though there’s a catch: softer metals like copper and brass can be damaged by the abrasives, so skip those. Silver jewelry is a great candidate, too. Avoid polished metals and soft stones like opals, pearls, or turquoise. “Always use a gentle hand and test first,” Ramos says. For walls, shoes, and more Crayon on painted walls is a classic small-kid problem. Toothpaste can lift it, but the wall finish matters. “Due to the mild abrasives in the paste, flat or matte paint may sometimes fade or become damaged,” Ramos says. “And on darker or more delicate finishes, it could leave dull spots or streaks.” Glossy, light-colored paint holds up well. Toothpaste also works on white rubber soles and leather or canvas sneakers. Just keep it away from suede, mesh, or anything delicate; those materials can stain or break down. For a persistent stain on a toilet seat, apply a small amount with a cloth or toothbrush, scrub gently, let it sit a few minutes, and wipe clean. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post 8 surprising household uses for toothpaste, from a pro cleaner first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: “Vibe coding,” is so last year. If you want to (try) to get on the same wavelength as teens and tweens, here’s another expression to add to your repertoire: Collins Dictionary has selected “mogging” as its 2026 word of the year. The slang term popular among Gen Z and Gen Alpha is defined as outperforming or outshining someone or something. Believed to be a shortened version of AMOG (alpha male of the group), the word traces back to bodybuilding culture around the 2010s. But it’s soared in popularity over the past year, with younger generations using it in a more playful way. Collins noted that experts found a 210% increase in usage of the “fast-growing slang word” in 2026, meriting the “word of the year” crown. So how do you use it? If your friend looks amazing in the selfie you just took, but your eyes are closed and hair is out of place — they’re mogging you. Or, to offer a more meta example, mogging is mogging the other words in the dictionary. Other words on the British dictionary’s shortlist include: Bixie : a haircut that’s shorter than a bob but longer than a pixie cut Fricy : a blend of fruity and spicy Friendslop : a low-budget, independently made video game designed to be played casually with friends Carspreading : the tendency of manufacturers to build cars that are longer, wider, and heavier Hydration break : a pause in a sporting contest to allow the contestants to drink fluids, especially in high heat Ghost job : a role advertised by an employer who has no intention of actually hiring anyone On Oct. 25, Dictionary.com announced its own word of the year: “Maxxing,” a shortened version of “maximizing” that can be used on its own or tacked on to the end of another word to describe the act of optimizing something. Derived from gamer lingo and in use for over a decade, the slang term broke through on TikTok in the 2020s. Its most famous usage is perhaps “looksmaxxing,” which refers to taking a person’s appearance to its full potential, but “sleepmaxxing,” “cozymaxxing,” and “booksmaxxing” have all joined the zeitgeist as well. “Really, anything in your life can get the maxxing treatment, if you do it wholeheartedly enough,” the online dictionary wrote in a blog post.

items.descriptionOriginal: P undits are describing last night as a romp for Democrats, a rebuke of Republicans, a blue tsunami, a rout in the red states. But underneath these headlines is a quieter, parallel story about voters choosing to abandon tribal allegiance and make decisions for themselves. For months, we’ve been hearing about the possibility of a blue wave — and then, in the same breath, the caveat: Is a wave even possible in today’s hyper-polarized America? And yet, in Texas, Florida, Kansas and beyond, the electorate refused to let party loyalty make their choice for them. Young, Latino and red-state voters moved, sometimes dramatically, in just two years. The composition of the two sides turned out to be less fixed than we imagined, with a meaningful number of voters willing to cast ballots across party lines when a candidate, issue or circumstance spoke to them. In Texas, where Democrats had historic wins, people of all parties have recently united to fight against a border wall through Big Bend National Park. Credit: Sam Karas Part of the story was turnout, said New York Times Chief Political Analyst Nate Cohn on The Daily . But, he added, “Many people who are registered as Republicans and voted for Donald Trump voted for the Democratic candidate.” This feels like a fitting conclusion to The Depolarization Project , our special series about how political polarization works and what we can do about it. The premise of that series was that depolarization isn’t about meeting in the middle. It’s about choosing to remain open and curious, rather than blindly clinging to arbitrary affiliations. In the end, many voters showed that their party label doesn’t have the final say. Data center opposition is proving to be a bipartisan, or even nonpartisan, issue across the U.S. Credit: Here Now / Shutterstock Wednesdays are normally “What We’re Reading” day here at Reasons to be Cheerful, so in that spirit, here’s a post-Election Day list of stories from our own depolarization series and from elsewhere around the web. We Hate to Break It to You, But Maybe We’re Not That Polarized – the New York Times A Wall Meant to Divide Is Uniting Left and Right in Texas – Reasons to be Cheerful Voters Vastly Underestimate the Open-Mindedness of Their Political Rivals – PsyPost The Door-to-Door Technique That Actually Changes Minds — Reasons to be Cheerful The post The Election That Transcended Tribalism appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: It is amazing how fallen leaves are helping feed over 1,200 students at IIT Bombay 🔥 With support from IIT Bombay-funded startup Infixen, nearly 2 tonnes of garden waste generated every day are being converted into fuel pellets that help power the kitchen at Hostel 16. This innovation has helped reduce LPG consumption by 60% while preparing meals for more than 1,200 students. The same garden waste that once cost the institute nearly ₹50 lakh every year to transport away is now becoming a valuable energy resource. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Walkable Traveler: Discovering Philadelphia’s Greenest Neighborhoods on Foot Reading Time: 3 minutes The Walkable Traveler: Discovering Philadelphia’s Greenest Neighborhoods on Foot There’s a moment on most city breaks when you realise you’ve spent more time getting between places than actually enjoying them. You’ve waited for a taxi, sat in traffic, arrived somewhere only to discover it’s a ten-minute walk from where you were half an hour ago. It’s enough to make you wonder why you bothered with the car in the first place. Philadelphia is a city where I’d be inclined to leave it behind.Not everywhere is within walking distance, obviously, but a surprising amount of the central area is. The streets are laid out in a fairly straightforward grid, and there’s plenty to see without travelling particularly far. I’d probably start somewhere around Independence Hall, partly because it’s one of those places you feel you ought to visit, and partly because the surrounding streets are worth a look in their own right. From there, Reading Terminal Market isn’t too far away. I wouldn’t bother making elaborate lunch plans. With that many food stalls under one roof, you’re almost certain to find something you fancy, although deciding what to eat might take longer than expected. Afterward, you could head towards Rittenhouse Square. I rather like the idea of a park that doesn’t try too hard to be an attraction. Rittenhouse is simply a pleasant place to sit for a while, with trees, benches and people going about their day. Somebody’s reading a book. Somebody else is walking a dog that clearly has no intention of going home yet. Meanwhile, the surrounding streets are full of shops, restaurants and apartments. It feels like a proper part of the neighbourhood rather than somewhere created exclusively for visitors. Philadelphia has quite a few green spaces like that, although some are much smaller. Community gardens are particularly interesting. You might find one occupying what was once an empty lot, with vegetables growing in raised beds and a few chairs tucked into a corner. They aren’t necessarily places you’d travel across the city to visit. But coming across one while walking through a residential neighbourhood is rather lovely. And they tell you something about the people who live there. I’d also make time for South Philadelphia. East Passyunk Avenue has the sort of mixture I enjoy: independent shops, restaurants, cafés and ordinary residential streets just around the corner. You can wander without feeling you’re missing some major attraction because you haven’t followed a particular route. The nearby Italian Market area is worth including too, especially if you like looking around food shops. I’d probably end up buying something completely impractical to carry around for the rest of the afternoon. One thing I wouldn’t do is try to squeeze all of Philadelphia into a single walking itinerary. It’s a sizeable city, and there’s no prize for finishing your holiday with sore feet. SEPTA’s buses, trolleys and trains make it possible to cover longer distances without needing a car, which is useful if you want to explore beyond the central neighbourhoods. Where you stay can make the whole thing easier or considerably more annoying. I once heard somebody describe a hotel as being ‘only twenty minutes from everything’, which sounds wonderful until you realise they meant twenty minutes by car. For a trip focused on walking, I’d be looking at the actual streets around the accommodation. Is there somewhere nearby for breakfast? Can you reach a park without crossing several major roads? How far is the nearest transit stop? Those details matter more to me than whether the apartment has an especially impressive television. One of the most effective ways to practice eco-friendly travel is reducing reliance on automobiles during city visits. Philadelphia’s grid layout makes it one of the most pedestrian- and transit-friendly cities in North America, allowing visitors to walk from historic landmarks to local farmers’ markets with ease. Choosing a neighborhood rental situated near public transportation hubs and neighborhood parks allows travelers to experience authentic community life while keeping emissions low. Rather than juggling multiple booking platforms, smart travelers use independent meta-search portals to find well-located accommodations. Exploring Philadelphia vacation rentals via cozycozy gives travelers real-time access to available townhomes, lofts, and historic suites across every major rental portal, making it effortless to lock in a sustainable home base. I’d check the final booking details separately, particularly the exact location and any additional charges. Of course, there’s an environmental benefit to doing more of a city break on foot. Fewer car journeys generally mean fewer transport emissions , and using public transport for longer trips can help reduce your reliance on taxis or a hire car. But I wouldn’t spend the whole weekend thinking about my carbon footprint.I’d be thinking about where to get another coffee, whether there’s time to explore one more street and why I hadn’t left myself longer at the market. That’s probably what makes walking such a good way to experience Philadelphia. You get to see the famous buildings, but you also spend time in the places between them. The little gardens, the corner shops, the streets where nothing especially remarkable is happening.And sometimes those are the bits you remember most. The post The Walkable Traveler: Discovering Philadelphia’s Greenest Neighborhoods on Foot appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: "Acting is not a real job that pays. How will you survive with theatre?" For Lalit, whose father drove an auto-rickshaw and whose mother was a homemaker, it was a difficult question to answer. He loved theatre, but his family worried about how he would earn a living from it. But passion is stubborn that way. Even when today's questions go unanswered, it stays. Lalit kept training with theatre groups across Delhi , often paying out of pocket, until a poster near Mandi House, the city's theatre district, caught his eye. It was for Bargad, a fellowship offering free training and a monthly stipend. He instantly knew where he had to be. "What's the harm in trying, I thought to myself and am I glad I did?" he recalls with glee. In January 2025, he joined its first cohort of 14 fellows and on day one, co-founder Amba asked them to write down what they hoped to gain from the programme. "She asked us to re-visit it after six months," Lalit says. Lalit, whose father drove an auto-rickshaw, chose the stage over certainty, and a poster led him to Bargad. He had hoped that the programme would lead him to a "well-known drama school" and return with a qualification he could show his family. So he wrote, folded the paper and slipped it into a pocket. His family's question was still unanswered. But it was one Bargad had been built to confront. Who gets to tell their stories? Behind the fellowship was a larger question: who gets to pursue theatre when training costs money, time and the security of a regular income? For Amba, Co-Founder of Bargad and Academic Head of the Fellowship, the journey into this question began with her own experience of the performing arts. After training at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art and working in London for five years, she returned to India with a desire to build a theatre practice of her own. The question for her wasn't just one of who gets access to theatre training and professional opportunities, but whose stories, imaginations and artistic voices get valued in the first place. Co-founder Amba questions who gets through theatre's door, and who has historically been told it belongs to them. "I realised there is heavy gatekeeping in the performing arts, and how much of it is shaped by caste and privilege - an accident of birth," she says. "Who gets through the door? And historically, who has been told that the door belongs to them? Bargad is an attempt to question that gatekeeping," Amba says For Anirudh, Co-Founder of Bargad and Course Director of the Fellowship, the question became personal about 10 years ago, while working on a play about the Criminal Tribes Act. Until then, he says, his privileged background had blinded him to many inequalities. "I was born into a privileged caste and class with access to education and exposure, and I lived most of my life in a little bubble, blind to everything around me," he tells The Better India. "That play was my first honest encounter with the reality of caste and with Ambedkar's writings. It felt as if everything I had learnt and believed was a lie. The ground beneath me shifted." Anirudh's encounter with caste while staging a play on the Criminal Tribes Act changed how he saw everything. In 2025, this led to the founding of Bargad by Amba-Suhasini K Jhala and Anirudh Nair, with Sanyukta Saha, who runs the Agaaz Theatre Trust, and Shambhavi Singh, founder of Oddbird Theatre. Its first cohort began in January 2025. For Amba, widening access meant more than inviting new people into existing institutions. It meant changing the conditions that decide who can enter at all. Paying students to make theatre possible There on, Bargad's first answer was practical: make training free and pay the people undertaking it. Sanyukta Saha, who has spent years bringing theatre to Delhi's Nizamuddin Basti through Aagaaz, and Shambhavi Singh, co-founder of Oddbird Theatre, helped found Bargad in 2025. The first two cohorts received ₹10,000 a month and the third, which begins January 2027, will receive ₹15,000. Classes run from 4 pm to 8.30 pm, six days a week, allowing fellows to earn during the day. Many applicants are financial contributors in their families , and attending classes can mean giving up hours they would otherwise spend working. "For the fellows, the opportunity cost of taking time out to train in the arts is quite high," Anirudh says. "The guarantee of a stipend also helps convince their families." Before joining, Lalit had paid to learn theatre and sometimes depended on his siblings for money. The stipend gave him a measure of financial independence. "For the first time, I was being paid to do theatre," he says. "Initially I was in disbelief but I knew this would be a great opportunity to afford what I enjoyed the most. With the stipend, I did not have to ask my brother or sister for money, and I spent it on travel, books and personal necessities." Fellows train from 4 pm to 8.30 pm, six days a week, leaving daylight hours free to earn. He did not tell his parents when he was selected; only his brother knew. The question of what theatre could offer him remained unresolved, but for the first time, he had room to find out. Bargad also challenges the assumption that a lack of formal training means a lack of ability. Applications grew from around 75 in the first year to about 200 in the second. Candidates can apply in English or Hindi through written or video submissions. An independent online jury shortlists around 30 applicants for three rigorous in-person audition rounds, followed by a group audition testing their listening, collaboration, responsiveness to direction and ensemble skills. A second jury selects the final 14. "We keep the batch deliberately small so that each fellow receives sustained individual attention, close mentorship and the space to take risks, experiment and grow within a close-knit ensemble," explains Amba. The six-month curriculum covers voice, movement, acting, improvisation, writing and devising, with visiting practitioners from Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and Chennai. The emphasis is not only on learning techniques, but on finding ways to use them to make original work. A scene is never really finished Neel Chaudhuri, a devising teacher who has taught at Bargad since its inception, works with fellows to develop performances from prompts in the subject of 'Devicing' or as he puts it, "to learn to learn to look within and ideate on what story one would like to tell independently." In devising labs with faculty member Neel Chaudhuri, fellows return to short scenes every fortnight, learning that ideas grow through process, not perfection. In 'Divising Labs' held every other week, fellows build short scenes and return to them over time, watching how an idea changes with further work. "The idea is not that they have to make a perfect scene in two weeks, but that they should follow a process, learn how a story is conceptualised and all that goes into seeing it to fruition," he says. The distinction is important. Rather than treating the first version of a scene as a finished product, the process encourages fellows to revisit their choices, test different approaches and discover what the work might become. The focus is on developing an idea, not simply producing something quickly. That approach also opens up what can count as material for theatre. "A scene need not begin with an extraordinary event or a fully formed story. An everyday object, a remembered incident or a private discomfort can become a starting point. The work lies in examining the experience and finding a way to communicate it to an audience," Neel explains. Classes are conducted mainly in Hindi, and faculty are asked to work bilingually. "Fellows can ask questions and experiment without feeling that they must already know the conventions of theatre. And language is a big part of it," he says. When life becomes the story For Prerna Bisht, who joined the fellowship in 2026 after an unsuccessful application the previous year, that process began with food. Prerna Bisht turned childhood shame about hidden meals into a story of caste, secrecy and social pressure, and felt liberated. During a workshop led by Vamsi, an interdisciplinary theatre artist who explores the layered relationship between caste and food, fellows were asked to tell stories through what they ate. The prompt took Prerna back to her childhood in Haryana, where her family's non-vegetarian food was treated as something to conceal. "My father would shut every door and window while cooking so that nobody would know what we were eating," she says. "Once, a neighbour's child walked in, and we hurriedly hid our plates. For a long time, I was ashamed of my food and I often ate my school lunch hidden from everyone," Prerna recalls with a tinge of sorrow in her voice. The memory was about more than a meal. It captured how the fear of being judged could follow someone beyond the home, turning an ordinary part of one's life into a source of embarrassment. The workshop gave Prerna a way to revisit that experience and examine what it had meant to her. "At Bargad, food became a way into a story about social pressure, secrecy and the shame I had carried into school. I felt liberated," she says. Here, a first draft is only a beginning, and every scene is allowed to change This is one of the possibilities of devising: experiences that might otherwise remain private can be shaped into material for performance. The process does not erase what happened. It gives the person telling the story a way to look at it differently and decide what they want to share. Taking the story to the stage After any programme, the question that often arises in the minds of students is: "What next?" In theatre, that anxiety can be manifold with scarce opportunities, rising costs and inaccessibility. To solve this, the founders began Bargad ka Chabutra , a further six-month programme that alumni can apply to. It includes masterclasses on running workshops, fundraising and producing, among other supportive teaching. Students can also apply for one of two production grants of Rs. 1 lakh each. Lalit's cohort used one grant to expand a 15-minute scene about manual scavenging into Hawa Mahal , a full-length play. The group interviewed manual scavengers, whose experiences informed the production. Lalit then became a part of a larger production team and designed a set made from pipes and windows that also doubled as manholes. Hawa Mahal grew from a fifteen-minute scene into a full-length play on manual scavenging, with pipes doubling as manholes. Over seven months, the students developed the production, learning not only how to shape a story but also how to organise the work needed to bring it to an audience. For Lalit, that meant taking on responsibilities beyond acting and helping turn the group's research into a stage production. Finding space for the story Getting a play on stage presented another challenge. Auditoriums around Mandi House can cost ₹80,000 to ₹1 lakh a day, while affordable independent venues are limited and often booked well in advance. Hawa Mahal had six performances, including one at Ashoka University. For Lalit, the response after one performance made the work feel worthwhile. "After three shows, in a post-show meeting, the audience told us thank you for telling this story," he says. But taking a story from the classroom to an audience requires funding, rehearsal time and space. The ability to develop a production is of little use if there is nowhere affordable to stage it. "In theatre, it is impossible to work without space, both to build work and to show it to audiences," Neel says. Behind every performance lies unseen work: rehearsal, research, affordable space and funding. Bargad has tried to address this by building a network of spaces, people and resources that can help the fellows bridge the gap. Nikhil Mehta of Black Box Okhla has hosted the fellowship and its alumni programme. Other fellows have continued their work in different ways: a graduate from a village in Bihar received a Rs. 1 lakh grant to write a play, a fellow from the second cohort joined the National School of Drama, and another won a full scholarship to Drama School Mumbai. Keeping the door open Bargad's future depends on making these opportunities sustainable. Over two years, the programme has relied on around 20 to 25 individual donors, contributing between Rs. 5,000 and Rs. 5 lakh. With Delhi auditoriums costing up to ₹1 lakh a day, affordable stage space remains theatre's quiet barrier. Their support has helped keep it running, but relying on individual generosity makes long-term planning difficult. "Sustainability is not about finding more well-wishers every year," Amba says. "It is about finding long-term partners who understand that access cannot depend on annual generosity, so we can plan three, four, five years ahead." With more stable funding, she hopes to establish year-long courses in every metro, tour productions and offer larger bursaries. These ambitions would expand the opportunities available to performers who might otherwise struggle to enter the field. Giving theatre a future By the end of the fellowship, the qualification Lalit had once hoped for no longer mattered to him. With Bargad, performers like Lalit no longer need a certificate, only the confidence to stage their next play on their own terms. Photograph: (All images courtesy of: Akshita Doley and Santwana Saira John) "I had so much confidence by then that I did not need a tag," he says. "I can proudly say that I studied in Bargad's first batch. Now, I don't even know where that piece of paper I wrote on is," he laughs. His family's question, how will you survive with theatre, still has no single answer. But Lalit now asks it as someone who has put a play on stage, and who is no longer waiting for anyone's permission to make the next one.

items.description: Οι επιστήμονες ανακάλυψαν μια ένωση που μετατρέπει μια φυσική πρωτεΐνη που επανορθώνει τους μυς σε μια πιο ισχυρή έκδοση που ονομάζεται «Super HGF», υπερδιπλασιάζοντας την ικανότητά της να δεσμεύεται σε έναν βασικό υποδοχέα ενώ την προστατεύει από χημική βλάβη που σχετίζεται με την ηλικία. Η ανακάλυψη, που υποστηρίχθηκε από πρώιμα πειράματα με ποντίκια, θα μπορούσε τελικά να βοηθήσει στην καταπολέμηση της απώλειας μυών και της προ…
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have discovered a compound that transforms a natural muscle-repair protein into a more powerful version dubbed "Super HGF," more than doubling its ability to bind to a key receptor while protecting it from age-related chemical damage. The breakthrough, supported by early mouse experiments, could eventually help combat muscle loss and preserve strength as people age.

items.descriptionOriginal: As more of the planet’s wild places are consumed by human sprawl, people are increasingly trying to protect wildlife by moving it out of harm’s way. While such relocations might help a construction project clear a regulatory hurdle, it’s often not doing much good for the wildlife, according to new research. Just 6% of amphibian and reptile relocations tied to development could be classified as successful, according to a review of such projects published recently in Conservation Biology . “Moving these species away from a construction site does not mean they will survive in their new home,” said Megan Winand , a University of British Columbia biologist and the lead author. The results offer a sobering look at the performance of this increasingly popular strategy, as development of everything from pipelines to parks clashes with species protections. And while the authors found evidence of ways to improve the performance of such transplant projects, the main takeaway is that it’s usually better to avoid destroying a wild animal’s home than moving the creature to a new one. “We need to prioritize protecting habitat and explore alternatives to current mitigation practices, which this review shows are often failing to achieve meaningful conservation outcomes,” said Winand. The scale of the issue is staggering. While there is no comprehensive count of how often critters are moved to make way for development, a separate 2026 study by many of the same authors found that in British Columbia alone, some 5.1 million amphibians and reptiles were moved just between 2019 and 2022. both;} Recommended Reading: As the world warms, butterflies are relocating at an astonishing scale The new study focuses on cases from around the world where at least something is known about how the transplanted animals fared. They scanned the scientific literature for papers published between 2007 and 2023 that examined the fate of relocated amphibians and reptiles. All told, they looked at 256 case studies tracking everything from tortoises to alligators. Most of the research was concentrated in North America, Europe, Australia and New Zealand. Nearly 70% of the translocations were done for conservation purposes, such as releasing an animal into habitat that it once occupied. The rest were cases involving animals moved to get them out of the way of development. The researchers then graded a relocation’s performance based on a four-tiered system. The first level was when the original transplants were surviving. A project reached level two when those survivors were reproducing. The third level came when the population was growing. The final, highest level was if a paper showed evidence that the population had achieved longterm viability. Based on that grading system, development-related relocations earned an abysmal grade. Just 6% of the cases were shown to have reached the third or fourth benchmarks. Nearly half of them failed to hit even the first level – that the original population had survived the move. While conservation-related transplants performed more than three times better, that still meant they only reached the top two levels 19% of the time. They had total failures in nearly a quarter of cases. A closer look at the different studies revealed two factors that seemed to contribute to the greater success of the conservation transplants, the scientists found. Things turned out better in cases where people tried to removed threats to an animal in the place where it was being relocated. Higher scores were also linked to more long-term monitoring after the move. “Without adequate follow-up, we won’t know whether animals survive in their new location, reproduce or establish a population that can survive over time,” says Winand. “Relocated animals may also leave the release sites, encounter new threats or face difficult habitat conditions.” So there are things people can do to increase the odds that the transplants will endure. The high failure rate of even the conservation-related measures shouldn’t be taken as a sign of poor execution by the people involved, the authors note. Rather, it illustrates how hard it is to do such translocations, especially for long-lived species that reproduce slowly. It also reinforces a common insight into biodiversity-related work: It’s a lot easier to avoid breaking something in the first place than to try to fix damage later.
